Both powers remain far removed from making laws and enforcing them through penalties touching property, liberty, limbs, and life. Command ends with minority. Afterwards, a son still always owes his parents honour and respect, support and defence, and everything gratitude can require for the greatest benefits nature allows him to receive. But none of this places a sceptre in the father's hand or grants sovereign command. He has no dominion over his son's property or actions, nor any right to dictate his son's will in everything. Even so, in many matters that cause little inconvenience to himself or his family, a son may properly defer to his father's wishes.

A person may owe honour and respect to an elderly or wise man; defence to his child or friend; relief and support to the distressed; and gratitude to a benefactor so great that everything he has and can do cannot repay it adequately. None of this gives anyone authority or the right to legislate over the person owing these duties. Plainly, these obligations do not arise simply from the title of father. That is not only because, as already said, the mother is owed them too. It is also because obligations to parents, and the degree of duty required from children, may vary with the care, kindness, trouble, and expense devoted more to one child than another.

This explains why parents in societies where they are themselves subjects retain power over their children and have as much right to their subjection as parents in the state of nature. That would be impossible if all political power were merely paternal and the two were really identical. All paternal power would then belong to the prince, and a subject could naturally possess none. Political and paternal powers, however, are entirely distinct and separate. They rest on different foundations and are given for different purposes. Every subject who is a father has as much paternal power over his children as the prince has over his. Every prince with living parents owes them as much filial duty and obedience as the humblest subject owes his own. Parental authority can therefore contain no part or degree of the dominion a prince or magistrate holds over a subject.

Parents' duty to raise their children and children's duty to honour their parents contain all the power on one side and submission on the other that properly belong to this relationship. Yet a father ordinarily has another power that gives him a hold on his children's obedience. He shares this power with other people, but occasions for exercising it occur almost constantly within fathers' own private families, while examples elsewhere are rare and less noticed. The world therefore treats it as part of paternal jurisdiction. It is people's general power to give their estates to those who please them most. Children normally expect to inherit their father's possessions in particular proportions fixed by each country's law and custom. Yet the father can commonly give more generously or sparingly according to how far each child's behaviour has suited his wishes and temper.

This is a considerable hold on children's obedience. Moreover, enjoying land always involves submission to the government of the country containing it. People have therefore commonly supposed that a father could bind his descendants to the government he himself obeyed, and that his agreement bound them. In fact, this submission is merely a necessary condition attached to the land. Inheriting an estate under that government binds only those willing to accept it on that condition. It is therefore voluntary submission, not a natural bond or commitment. Everyone's children are naturally as free as he is, or as any ancestor ever was. While they remain free, they may choose which society to join and which commonwealth to live under. But if they want their ancestors' inheritance, they must accept it on the same terms and submit to every condition attached to its possession. Through this power, fathers do indeed induce obedience even from adult children and usually subject them to one political power or another. Neither result comes from a special right of fatherhood. It comes from the reward in their hands with which they enforce and repay compliance. This gives no more power than a French man has over an English man whose obedience he strongly secures by the prospect of an estate he will leave him. If the English man wishes to enjoy that estate once inherited, he must accept the conditions attached to landownership in its country, whether France or England.

To conclude, a father's command extends only through his children's minority, and only as far as the discipline and government appropriate to that age. Throughout their lives and in every condition, children indispensably owe their parents honour, respect, and all that the Latins called piety, together with support and defence. Yet none of this gives a father governing power—that is, power to make laws and impose penalties on his children—or dominion over his son's property and actions. Nevertheless, we can readily understand how a family's father could become its prince in the world's earliest ages.* The same can happen where sparse populations still allow families to separate into unoccupied regions and settle in vacant places. The father had ruled from his children's infancy. Since living together would be difficult without government, it was most likely to remain with him through the children's express or tacit consent after they grew up. It seemed simply to continue unchanged. In reality, they needed only to permit the father alone to exercise within the family the executive power of the law of nature that naturally belongs to every free man. By that permission, they gave him monarchical power while remaining in the family. This plainly arose from the children's consent rather than any paternal right. Nobody doubts that if a stranger brought there by chance or business killed one of the children or committed another offence, the father could condemn and execute or otherwise punish him just as he could a child. He could not do so through paternal authority over someone who was not his child. He acted through the executive power of the law of nature, to which he was entitled as a man. He alone could punish within his family because his children, out of respect, had set aside their own exercise of that power. They yielded to the dignity and authority they willingly allowed him above the rest of the family.

(*It is no improbable opinion therefore, which the archphilosopher was of, that the chief person in every houshold was always, as it were, a king: so when numbers of housholds joined themselves in civil societies together, kings were the first kind of governors amongst them, which is also, as it seemeth, the reason why the name of fathers continued still in them, who, of fathers, were made rulers; as also the ancient custom of governors to do as Melchizedec, and being kings, to exercise the office of priests, which fathers did at the first, grew perhaps by the same occasion. Howbeit, this is not the only kind of regiment that has been received in the world. The inconveniences of one kind have caused sundry others to be devised; so that in a word, all public regiment, of what kind soever, seemeth evidently to have risen from the deliberate advice, consultation and composition between men, judging it convenient and behoveful; there being no impossibility in nature considered by itself, but that man might have lived without any public regiment, Hooker’s Eccl. Pol. lib. i. sect. 10.)

It was therefore easy and almost natural for children, through tacit and scarcely avoidable consent, to give way to their father's authority and government. In childhood they had grown used to following his directions and bringing their small disputes to him. Once they became adults, who was better suited to rule them? Their small properties and still smaller greed seldom produced greater quarrels. When such quarrels arose, where could they find a better arbitrator than the man whose care had sustained and raised every one of them, and who felt tenderness towards them all? No wonder they drew no distinction between minority and adulthood, or looked for twenty-one or another age to make them free to dispose of themselves and their fortunes. They could have no wish to escape their tutelage. The government they had lived under continued to protect more than restrain them. Nowhere could they find greater security for their peace, liberties, and fortunes than under their father's rule.

Thus, through an almost imperceptible change, the natural fathers of families became their political monarchs too. Depending on whether they lived long and left able, worthy heirs over several generations, or whether things went otherwise, they founded hereditary or elective kingdoms. These developed different constitutions and customs as chance, planning, and circumstances shaped them. But suppose princes hold their titles by their fathers' right, and fathers' natural claim to political authority is sufficiently proved because we commonly find them actually exercising government. If that argument holds, I say, it proves just as strongly that all princes—indeed, princes alone—should be priests. For it is as certain that in the beginning the family's father was its priest as that he was ruler in his own household.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 — Of Political or Civil Society
paragraphs: God made man a creature for whom, in his own judgment, being alone was not good. He therefore placed him under strong pressures of need, convenience, and inclination that drove him into society, while giving him understanding and language to sustain and enjoy it. The first society joined husband and wife, giving rise to the society of parents and children. In time, the relationship between master and servant was added. These relationships could, and commonly did, combine in one family, whose master or mistress exercised a kind of rule appropriate to a household. Yet neither separately nor together did they amount to political society. We shall see this by considering their different purposes, bonds, and limits.

Marital society is formed through a voluntary agreement between a man and a woman. Its chief element is the sharing of, and right to, one another's bodies required for its principal purpose, procreation. Yet it also brings mutual support and assistance and shared interests. These are needed not merely to unite their care and affection, but also for their common offspring, who have a right to nourishment and support from them until able to provide for themselves.

The purpose of joining male and female is not simply procreation but the species' continuation. Their union should therefore continue after procreation for as long as their young need nourishment and support. Those who begot them must sustain them until they can fend and provide for themselves. We find the lower creatures consistently obeying this rule, which the infinitely wise maker gave his works. Among grass-eating animals that bear live young, the union of male and female lasts only for mating itself. The mother's milk sufficiently nourishes the young until they can feed on grass. The male merely begets them and takes no further concern for mother or offspring, whose support he cannot help provide. Among beasts of prey, however, the union lasts longer. Hunting is both more laborious and more dangerous than grazing, and the mother cannot readily support herself and nourish her numerous offspring through her own catches alone. The male's assistance is therefore needed to maintain their common family. Until the young can hunt for themselves, they depend on both parents' joint care. The same holds for all birds, except certain domestic ones whose abundant food excuses the cock from feeding and caring for the brood. Because the young need food in the nest, cock and hen remain mates until the young can use their wings and provide for themselves.

Here, I think, lies the chief, perhaps the only, reason why human males and females remain bound together longer than other creatures. The woman can conceive again, and in fact commonly becomes pregnant and gives birth again long before the earlier child stops depending on parental support. That child cannot yet fend for himself and has not received all the assistance his parents owe him. The father, bound to care for those he has begotten, must therefore remain in marital society with the same woman longer than other creatures do. Their young can support themselves before the next breeding season; the marital bond then dissolves of itself, and they are free until Hymen summons them in his usual annual season to choose new mates. We cannot help admiring the great Creator's wisdom here. He gave human beings foresight and the ability to store up for the future as well as meet present needs. He also made a longer union necessary between husband and wife than between male and female in other creatures. This encourages their industry and more firmly joins their interests in providing and accumulating goods for their common offspring. Uncertain pairings or easy, frequent dissolutions of marriage would greatly disrupt that provision.

These obligations bind humanity and make human marital bonds firmer and longer-lasting than those found in the other animal species. Yet we may still ask why this agreement cannot, like other voluntary agreements, be made terminable by consent, at a fixed time, or under specified conditions, provided procreation, education, and inheritance are secured. Neither its nature nor its purposes necessarily require it always to last for life. I mean, of course, people who are not bound by a positive law requiring every such contract to be permanent.

Although husband and wife share one common interest, they have different understandings and will inevitably sometimes have different wishes. Final decision—that is, rule—must therefore rest somewhere. It naturally falls to the man, as the more capable and stronger. But this concerns only their shared interests and property. The wife retains full and free possession of whatever belongs specifically to her by contract, and the husband has no more power over her life than she has over his. His power is so far from an absolute monarch's that in many cases she is free to separate from him where natural right or their contract permits. This holds whether they made the contract themselves in the state of nature or it follows their country's customs or laws. On separation, the children go to father or mother as that contract determines.

Every purpose of marriage can be achieved under political government as well as in the state of nature. The civil magistrate therefore does not reduce either party's rights or powers naturally necessary to those purposes: procreation, and mutual support and assistance while they remain together. He merely settles disputes between husband and wife about them. Suppose instead that absolute sovereignty and power over life and death naturally belonged to the husband and were necessary to marital society. Marriage could then not exist in countries denying husbands that absolute authority. But marriage's purposes require no such power. The marital relationship therefore does not confer it on the husband, since it is entirely unnecessary to that condition. Marital society could exist and fulfil its purposes without it. Indeed, shared goods and authority over them, mutual assistance and support, and other elements of marriage may be varied and regulated by the contract uniting husband and wife, as far as is consistent with procreation and raising children until they can fend for themselves. Nothing is necessary to a society unless it is necessary to the purposes for which that society is formed.

I discussed the society of parents and children, and their respective rights and powers, so fully in the preceding chapter that nothing more need be said here. I think it is clear that this society differs greatly from political society.

“Master” and “servant” are names as old as history, but they apply to people in very different conditions. A free man becomes another's servant by selling, for a fixed period, the service he undertakes in exchange for wages. This commonly brings him into his master's family and under its ordinary discipline, but gives the master only temporary power, extending no further than their contract provides. Another kind of servant bears the special name of slave. Captured in a just war, slaves are subjected by natural right to their masters' absolute dominion and arbitrary power. These men have, as I say, forfeited their lives, their liberties with them, and their estates. In slavery they cannot possess any property. They therefore cannot, in that condition, count as members of civil society, whose principal purpose is preserving property.

Consider, then, a family master with all these subordinate relationships—wife, children, servants, and slaves—combined under household rule. However closely the family's arrangement, offices, and even numbers resemble a small political commonwealth, its constitution, power, and purpose are very different. If we must call it a monarchy and its paterfamilias an absolute monarch, absolute monarchy will possess only fragmented and narrow power. As already shown, the family master has a distinct power over each of its various people, limited differently in duration and extent. Except over the slave, he has no legislative power of life and death over any of them, nor any power that a family's mistress could not also have. And the family remains just as much a family, and his power as paterfamilias just as great, whether it includes slaves or not. Someone whose power over each individual is strictly limited certainly cannot hold absolute power over the entire family. We shall best understand how a family, or any other human association, differs from properly political society by considering what political society itself consists in.

As proved already, everyone is born entitled to perfect freedom and unrestricted enjoyment of all the rights and privileges of the law of nature, equally with every other person or group in the world. Nature therefore gives him power not only to preserve his property—that is, his life, liberty, and estate—against others' injuries and attacks, but also to judge and punish their breaches of that law as he believes the offence deserves. This extends even to death where, in his judgment, the crime's seriousness requires it. Yet political society cannot exist or continue without power to preserve property and, for that purpose, punish its members' offences. Political society therefore exists only where every member has surrendered this natural power to the community in every case that leaves him able to appeal for protection to its established law. Each member's private judgment is thus set aside, and the community becomes arbitrator. It acts through settled, standing rules, impartial and identical for every party, and through people authorized by the community to execute them. It settles disputes over rights between society's members and punishes offences against society with the penalties established by law. We can therefore readily distinguish those who share political society from those who do not. People united in one body, with a common established law and a judiciary to which they can appeal, empowered to settle disputes and punish offenders, are in civil society together. Those without such a common appeal—I mean on earth—remain in the state of nature. Where no other judge exists, each judges for himself and executes his own judgment. As I have shown, this is the complete state of nature.

In this way the commonwealth acquires power to decide what punishment should apply to the various offences committed among its members which they consider deserving of punishment. This is the power of making laws. It also acquires power to punish any injury done to one of its members by someone outside the society. This is the power of war and peace. All this serves to preserve the property of every member of that society as far as possible. Anyone who enters civil society and becomes a member of a commonwealth thereby gives up his power to punish offences against the law of nature by acting on his own private judgment. But when he gives judgment of offences to the legislative in every case where he can appeal to the magistrate, he also gives the commonwealth a right to employ his force in executing its judgments whenever he is called upon. These are indeed his own judgments, since they are made by himself or his representative. Here we find the origin of civil society's legislative and executive power: to judge by standing laws how far offences committed within the commonwealth should be punished, and to determine through particular judgments founded on the circumstances of each case how far injuries from outside should be answered. In both matters, when the need arises, it may employ the full force of all its members.

Political or civil society exists, therefore, only where people unite in one society and each gives up his executive power under the law of nature, surrendering it to the public. This happens whenever people in the state of nature form one people, one body politic, under a single supreme government, or whenever someone joins and becomes part of an existing government. He thereby authorizes the society—or, what amounts to the same thing, its legislative—to make laws for him as the public good requires. He owes assistance in executing them just as he would his own decrees. This takes people out of the state of nature and into a commonwealth by establishing an earthly judge with authority to settle every dispute and remedy injuries suffered by any member. That judge is the legislative or the magistrates it appoints. Wherever people, however associated, lack such a decisive authority to appeal to, they remain in the state of nature.

It is therefore clear that absolute monarchy, which some people regard as the only form of government anywhere in the world, is actually incompatible with civil society and cannot be a form of civil government at all. Civil society exists to avoid and remedy the difficulties of the state of nature that necessarily follow when everyone judges his own case. It establishes a recognized authority to which every member can appeal over any injury received or dispute that arises, and which every member must obey.* People who lack such an authority to settle their differences remain in the state of nature. So does every absolute prince in relation to those under his dominion.

(*“The public power of any society stands above every person within that society. Its principal use is to give laws to all those subject to it. In such cases we must obey those laws unless reasons necessarily establish that the law of reason, or of God, commands the contrary.” Hook. Eccl. Pol. l. i. sect. 16.)

The prince is supposed to possess all legislative and executive power alone. Consequently, no judge is available, and nobody can appeal to an authority that will decide fairly and impartially and provide relief or redress for injuries or difficulties caused by the prince or his orders. Whatever his title—Czar, Grand Seignior, or anything else—such a ruler is as much in the state of nature with those under his dominion as with the rest of humanity. Whenever two people lack a standing rule and common earthly judge to settle disputes about their rights, they remain in the state of nature* with all its difficulties. The subject, or rather slave, of an absolute prince suffers this additional misery: in the ordinary state of nature, he is free to judge his own rights and defend them as best he can. But when his monarch's will and orders invade his property, he has not merely lost the appeal that members of society ought to possess. As though degraded beneath the common condition of rational creatures, he is denied freedom to judge or defend his own rights. He is exposed to every misery and disadvantage one could fear from someone who remains unrestricted in the state of nature, yet is corrupted by flattery and armed with power.

(*“There was only one way to remove such mutual grievances, injuries, and wrongs”—that is, those accompanying people in the state of nature—“and that was to reach agreement among themselves, establish some kind of public government, and submit to it. Those granted authority to rule and govern could then secure the peace, tranquillity, and happiness of the rest. People always knew they could defend themselves when confronted with force and injury. They knew that however much people might pursue their own advantage, doing so by injuring others must not be tolerated, but resisted by everyone through every proper means. Finally, they knew that nobody could reasonably determine his own right and proceed to defend it according to his own decision, since everyone favours himself and those he greatly loves. Disputes and troubles would therefore continue endlessly unless all gave their common consent to be governed by people they agreed upon. Without that consent, no reason would justify one person's setting himself up as another's lord or judge.” Hooker’s Eccl. Pol. l. i. sect. 10.)

Anyone who thinks absolute power purifies people's blood and corrects the baseness of human nature need only read this age's history, or any other's, to learn otherwise. Someone insolent and harmful in America's woods would probably be little better on a throne. There, learning and religion might be found to justify everything he did to his subjects, and the sword would promptly silence anyone daring to question it. To see what protection absolute monarchy provides, what fathers of their countries it makes of princes, and how happy and secure civil society becomes where this government reaches perfection, one need only consult the recent account of Ceylon.

In absolute monarchies, as in other governments, subjects can indeed appeal to laws and judges to settle disputes and restrain violence among themselves. Everyone considers this necessary and believes anyone trying to remove it deserves to be called an open enemy of society and humanity. Yet we have reason to doubt whether this springs from true love of society and mankind, or from the charity we all owe one another. It is no more than anyone who loves his own power, profit, or greatness may and naturally must do: keep the animals labouring and toiling solely for his pleasure and advantage from injuring or destroying each other. He cares for them out of love for himself and their profit to him, not love for them. Ask what security or defence exists in such a state against the absolute ruler's violence and oppression, and the question itself is scarcely tolerated. They are ready to tell you that merely asking for safety deserves death. They grant that between subjects there must be rules, laws, and judges to preserve mutual peace and security. But the ruler must be absolute and above such arrangements. Because he can inflict greater harm and wrong, it becomes right when he does so. Asking for protection against injury from the strongest hand is immediately called faction and rebellion. It is as though, on leaving the state of nature for society, people agreed that everyone except one person should be bound by law, while he kept all the freedom of the state of nature, enlarged by power and made lawless by impunity. This supposes people foolish enough to guard against harm from pole-cats and foxes, yet content—even imagining themselves safe—to be devoured by lions.

Whatever flatterers say to distract people's understanding, they cannot stop them feeling. When people discover that someone, whatever his station, stands outside their civil society's bounds, and that no earthly appeal protects them against his injuries, they tend to recognize that they remain in the state of nature in relation to him. As soon as possible, they seek the safety and security for which civil society was originally established and for which alone they entered it. Perhaps at first, as the following part of this discussion will show more fully, an exceptionally good man gained precedence over the rest. They deferred to his goodness and virtue as a kind of natural authority. By tacit consent, chief rule and arbitration of disputes fell to him, without safeguards beyond their confidence in his honesty and wisdom. Time then gave authority, and what some would call sacredness, to customs begun in the careless, unthinking innocence of the earliest ages. Successors of a different kind appeared. People discovered their property was unsafe under the government as it then stood, although government's sole purpose is preserving property.* They could never feel safe or at ease, or consider themselves in civil society, until legislative power was placed in collective bodies—senate, parliament, or whatever name you choose. Every individual then became subject to the laws he had helped establish as a member of the legislative, equally with the humblest person. Once a law was made, nobody could use his own authority to escape its force, or claim exemption through supposed superiority to excuse his own or his dependants' misconduct.** Nobody in civil society can be exempt from its laws. If someone may do whatever he pleases, with no earthly appeal for redress or protection against his harm, I ask whether he does not remain wholly in the state of nature and therefore outside that civil society. The alternative is to call the state of nature and civil society identical. I have never found anyone so devoted to anarchy as to affirm that.

(*“At first, once a particular form of government had been appointed, perhaps no further thought was given to how it should operate. Everything was left to the rulers' wisdom and discretion, until experience revealed this to be deeply inconvenient for all sides. What had been devised as a remedy actually aggravated the wound it should have healed. They saw that living by one person's will caused everyone's misery. This forced them to adopt laws in which everyone could see their duties beforehand and know the penalties for breaking them.” Hooker’s Eccl. Pol. l. i. sect. 10.)
(**“Civil law is an act of the entire body politic, and therefore governs each individual part of that same body.” Hooker, ibid.)

chapters.title: Chapter 8 — Of the Beginning of Political Societies
paragraphs: As already explained, all people are naturally free, equal, and independent. Nobody can be removed from this condition and subjected to another person's political power without his own consent. The only way to give up natural liberty and accept the bonds of civil society is to agree with others to join together in a community. They do this to live comfortably, safely, and peacefully together, enjoying their property securely and gaining greater protection against outsiders. Any number may do this without injuring the freedom of those who remain outside; those others retain the liberty of the state of nature. When people consent in this way to form one community or government, they immediately become a single body politic. Within that body, the majority has the right to act and bind the rest.

When a number of people form a community with the consent of every individual among them, they create one body with the power to act as one body. This can happen only through the majority's will and decision. The consent of its individual members is the only force that moves any community, and a single body must move in one direction. It must therefore move where the greater force carries it: the consent of the majority. Otherwise it could neither act nor continue as the single body and community that every individual agreed to form. Everyone is consequently bound by that consent to accept the majority's decision. Thus, in assemblies authorized by positive laws, where the authorizing law specifies no required number, the majority's act counts as the act of the whole. It naturally determines the decision, possessing the whole body's power under the law of nature and reason.

By consenting with others to form one body politic under one government, everyone therefore undertakes an obligation to every other member to submit to the majority's decision and be bound by it. Otherwise the original agreement joining them in one society would mean nothing and would not be an agreement at all. He would remain free of any obligations beyond those he already had in the state of nature. Where would there be any agreement, or any new commitment, if society's decisions bound him only as far as he personally chose and actually consented? He would retain precisely the liberty he had before the agreement, or that anyone else in the state of nature possesses: freedom to submit and consent to any of its acts whenever he pleases.

If reason does not allow the majority's consent to count as the whole body's act and bind every individual member, then only everyone's consent can make anything an act of the whole. Yet such consent is almost impossible to obtain. Illness and the demands of business inevitably keep many away from public assemblies, even in groups much smaller than a commonwealth. Add the different opinions and conflicting interests unavoidable in every collection of people, and entering society on these terms would resemble Cato's entering the theatre merely to leave it again. Such a constitution would make the mighty Leviathan shorter-lived than the feeblest creatures, unable to survive even the day of its birth. We cannot suppose this unless we believe rational creatures want to establish societies merely to dissolve them. Where the majority cannot bind the rest, the members cannot act as one body and will immediately dissolve again.

Anyone who leaves the state of nature to unite in a community must therefore be understood to surrender to the majority all the power needed for the purposes of that union, unless the members expressly agree on a number greater than a majority. Simply agreeing to form one political society accomplishes this. That is the entire agreement that exists, or needs to exist, between the individuals who enter or compose a commonwealth. Nothing begins and actually constitutes political society, then, except the consent of free people, numerous enough to form a majority, to unite and incorporate themselves into it. This, and this alone, has given or could give rise to any lawful government in the world.

I find two objections raised against this account. First, history offers no examples of a group of independent people, equal to one another, meeting together and beginning or establishing a government in this way.
Second, people cannot rightfully do this, because everyone is born under a government and must submit to it. They are therefore not free to establish a new government.

The answer to the first objection is that we should not be surprised by how little history tells us about people living together in the state of nature. The difficulties of that condition, together with their desire and need for society, brought groups together; if they intended to remain together, they promptly formed a community. If the lack of accounts means we cannot suppose people ever lived in the state of nature, we might equally suppose the soldiers in Salmanasser's or Xerxes's armies were never children, since we hear little about them until they were grown and assembled in armies. Government everywhere precedes records. Writing seldom appears among a people until civil society has long used more immediately necessary arts to secure their safety, comfort, and abundance. Only then do they investigate their founders' history and search for their origins, after living memory of them has disappeared. Commonwealths, like individuals, usually know little of their own birth and infancy. Whatever they know of their beginnings depends on records others happened to preserve. The accounts we do possess of political beginnings, except those of the Jews, where God intervened directly and which offer no support to paternal dominion, either plainly show the kind of beginning I have described or bear unmistakable traces of it.

Someone must have a remarkable determination to deny obvious facts whenever they conflict with his hypothesis if he refuses to admit that Rome and Venice began when people free and independent of one another united together. None had natural superiority over the others or owed them subjection. And if we may trust Josephus Acosta, he tells us that many parts of America had no government at all.

“There are great and apparent conjectures,” he says of the people of Peru, “that these men, for a long time had neither kings nor commonwealths, but lived in troops, as they do this day in Florida, the Cheriquanas, those of Brazil, and many other nations, which have no certain kings, but as occasion is offered, in peace or war, they choose their captains as they please,” 1. i. c. 25.

If someone says each man there was born subject to his father or family head, I have already proved that a child's duty to his father did not remove his freedom to join whatever political society he chose. In any case, these people were plainly free in practice. Whatever superiority some political writers now assign to individuals among them, those individuals made no such claim themselves. By consent they remained equal until, through the same consent, they appointed rulers. Their political societies therefore all began through voluntary union and mutual agreement among people freely choosing their governors and forms of government.

I hope it will also be admitted that those who left Sparta with Palantus, mentioned by Justin, 1. iii. c. 4., were free men independent of one another who established government over themselves by their own consent. I have thus supplied several historical examples of free people in the state of nature meeting, incorporating themselves, and founding a commonwealth. If the absence of examples proves that governments did not and could not begin this way, advocates of paternal empire would do better to leave that argument alone than use it against natural liberty. If they can produce as many historical examples of governments founded on paternal right, I think we could safely concede their case—although arguing from what happened to what ought rightfully to happen is weak at best. Were I to advise them, however, I would suggest that they avoid examining governments' actual beginnings too closely. They may discover at the foundations of most something very unfavourable to their purpose and to the power they defend.

To conclude, reason clearly supports our claim that people are naturally free. Historical examples show that the governments of the world established peacefully rested on that foundation and were created through the people's consent. There is therefore little room to doubt either where the right lies or what humanity has thought and practised concerning the original establishment of governments.

I do not deny that, looking back as far as history permits towards commonwealths' origins, we generally find them governed and administered by one man. I also readily believe that government commonly began with the father where a family was large enough to support itself and stayed together without mixing with others—as often happens where land is plentiful and people few. Under the law of nature, the father had the same power as anyone else to punish breaches of that law as he thought appropriate. He could therefore punish offending children even after they became adults and left his guardianship. They would very likely submit, and each would join him against an offender in turn. This gave him power to execute judgment on every transgression, effectively making him lawgiver and governor over everyone who remained with the family. He was the most suitable person to trust. Paternal affection protected their property and interests in his care, and their childhood habit of obedience made submission to him easier than submission to anyone else. If they needed a ruler, as people living together can hardly avoid government, who was likelier than their common father—unless negligence, cruelty, or another bodily or mental defect made him unfit? But suppose the father died and his immediate heir lacked the age, wisdom, courage, or other qualities needed to rule; or suppose several families met and agreed to remain together. They undoubtedly used their natural freedom to appoint whoever seemed most capable and most likely to govern well. Accordingly, among the peoples of America who remained beyond the conquering swords and expanding dominion of the great empires of Peru and Mexico, and thus enjoyed natural freedom, we find this practice: although caeteris paribus they usually prefer their dead king's heir, they pass him over if weak or incapable in any respect and appoint the strongest and bravest man as ruler.

Thus, however far records let us trace the peopling of the world and the histories of its nations, we commonly find government in one person's hands. This does not contradict what I affirm: political society begins when individuals consent to join together and form one society. Once incorporated in this way, they may establish whatever form of government they judge appropriate. Yet this circumstance has led people into the mistake of supposing that government is naturally monarchical and belongs to the father. It may therefore be useful to consider why people generally chose that form at the beginning. A father's prominence may indeed have helped establish some commonwealths and initially placed power in one hand. But paternal authority plainly was not the consideration that kept government in a single person's hands. Small monarchies—that is, almost all monarchies near their beginnings—have commonly been elective, at least on occasion.

First, in the earliest times the government exercised by a father over his children while they were young accustomed all those descended from him to living under the rule of one person. It taught them that such rule, exercised skilfully and carefully, with love and affection towards those governed, could secure and preserve all the political happiness they sought in society. No wonder they chose and naturally adopted the government familiar from infancy, which experience had shown to be comfortable and safe. Monarchy was also simple and the most obvious form to people whom experience had not instructed in alternative governments. Neither rulers' ambition nor their arrogance had yet taught them to guard against encroachments of prerogative or the difficulties of absolute power that hereditary monarchy tended to claim and impose. It is therefore unsurprising that they gave little thought to restraining the excesses of those they authorized to govern, or to balancing governmental power by dividing its parts among different hands. They had not experienced tyranny's oppression. Neither the age's customs nor their possessions and way of life, which offered little scope for greed or ambition, gave them reason to fear or guard against it. They naturally adopted a form of government that was not merely the simplest and most obvious, as I said, but also best suited to their existing circumstances. They needed protection against foreign invasions and injuries more than numerous laws. An equally simple and poor way of life kept their desires within the narrow limits of each person's small property and produced few disputes. With few offences and offenders, they needed neither many laws to settle controversies nor a variety of officials to supervise proceedings and execute justice. People who liked one another enough to form a society must also have had some acquaintance, friendship, and mutual trust. They therefore feared outsiders more than each other. Their first concern must have been protection against external force. It was natural to choose the government best suited to that purpose and appoint the wisest and bravest man to conduct their wars, lead them against their enemies, and govern them chiefly in that capacity.

Thus the kings of the Indians in America are little more than their armies' generals. America still provides a pattern of Asia and Europe's earliest ages, when inhabitants were few relative to the land, and the scarcity of people and money gave no incentive to enlarge estates or fight for wider territory. Although these kings command absolutely in war, they exercise little dominion at home in peacetime and possess only very moderate sovereignty. Decisions about peace and war ordinarily belong either to the people or to a council. War itself, however, cannot accommodate several commanders and therefore naturally places command solely in the king's hands.

Even in Israel, the principal task of the judges and earliest kings seems to have been commanding in war and leading armies. “Going out and in before the people” meant marching to war and returning at the head of their forces; the story of Jephtha makes this especially clear. When the Ammonites attacked Israel, the frightened Gileadites sent for Jephtha, a bastard of their family whom they had rejected. They agreed to make him ruler if he helped them against the Ammonites. The account says, “And the people made him head and captain over them,” Judg. xi, 11. This apparently meant the same as making him judge: “And he judged Israel,” judg. xii. 7.—that is, he was their captain-general for six years. Similarly, when Jotham reminded the Shechemites of their debt to Gideon, their judge and ruler, he said, “He fought for you, and adventured his life far, and delivered you out of the hands of Midian,” Judg. ix. 17. Nothing is mentioned beyond his service as general, and indeed that is all his history or the histories of the other judges contain. Abimelech is specifically called king, though at most he was their general. Later, tired of Samuel's sons' misconduct, the children of Israel wanted a king like other nations, “to judge them, and to go out before them, and to fight their battles,” I. Sam viii. 20. Granting their request, God told Samuel, “I will send thee a man, and thou shalt anoint him to be captain over my people Israel, that he may save my people out of the hands of the Philistines,” ix. 16. It is as though a king's sole business were leading their armies and fighting in their defence. Accordingly, at Saul's inauguration Samuel poured a vial of oil over him and declared that the Lord had anointed him “to be captain over his inheritance,” x. 1. After the tribes solemnly chose and acclaimed Saul king at Mispah, those unwilling to accept him raised only this objection: “How shall this man save us?” v. 27. They meant that he lacked the military skill and leadership needed to defend them and was therefore unfit to be king. When God decided to transfer government to David, he said, “But now thy kingdom shall not continue: the Lord hath sought him a man after his own heart, and the Lord hath commanded him to be captain over his people,” xiii. 14.—as though royal authority consisted entirely in being their general. Thus the tribes that had remained loyal to Saul's family and opposed David came to Hebron offering submission. Among their reasons for accepting him as king, they said he had effectively been their king during Saul's reign, leaving them no reason not to accept him now. “Also,” they said, “in time past, when Saul was king over us, thou wast he that reddest out and broughtest in Israel, and the Lord said unto thee, Thou shalt feed my people Israel, and thou shalt be a captain over Israel.”

Perhaps a family gradually developed into a commonwealth, with the father's authority continuing in the eldest son. Each person in turn grew up under that authority and tacitly submitted to it. Its mildness and equality offended nobody, so everyone accepted it until time seemed to confirm and establish a right of succession through long usage. Or perhaps several families, or their descendants, came together through chance, neighbourhood, or business and united in society. They needed a general whose leadership could defend them against their enemies in war. The innocence and sincerity of that poor but virtuous age—like almost every age founding governments that endure in the world—also gave people great confidence in one another. These founders therefore generally placed rule in one person's hands without express restrictions beyond those required by government's nature and purpose. Whichever process first established one-man rule, the power was certainly entrusted only for public good and safety. Its holders commonly used it for those purposes in commonwealths' infancy. Otherwise young societies could not have survived. Without such nurturing fathers, tenderly and carefully attending to public welfare, every government would have succumbed to the weakness of infancy, and prince and people would soon have perished together.

The golden age, before vain ambition and amor sceleratus habendi—evil desire for possessions—corrupted people's understanding of true power and honour, had more virtue, hence better governors and less vicious subjects. Rulers did not stretch prerogative to oppress the people; consequently, the people did not dispute privileges to reduce or restrain the magistrate's power. Rulers and people therefore did not contend over governors or government. But in later ages,* ambition and luxury sought to retain and enlarge power without performing the work for which it was given. Flattery helped teach princes to pursue interests separate from their people's. People then found it necessary to examine government's origins and rights more carefully and devise ways to restrain excessive power and prevent its abuse. They had entrusted that power to another solely for their own good, but found it being used to harm them.

(*“At first, once a particular form of government was approved, perhaps no further thought was given to how it should operate. Everything was left to the rulers' wisdom and discretion, until experience revealed this to be deeply inconvenient for all sides. What had been devised as a remedy actually aggravated the wound it should have healed. They saw that living by one person's will caused everyone's misery. This forced them to adopt laws in which everyone could see their duties beforehand and know the penalties for breaking them.” Hooker’s Eccl. Pol. l. i. sect. 10.)

We can therefore see how likely it was that naturally free people, who by their own consent either accepted their father's government or joined other families to establish government, would generally entrust rule to one man. They chose one person's leadership without even expressly limiting or regulating his power, believing his honesty and prudence sufficient safeguards. Yet they never imagined monarchy to be lure Divino, a doctrine unheard of among humanity until the theology of the last age revealed it to us. Nor did they grant paternal power a right to dominion or make it the foundation of all government. This should suffice to show that, as far as history sheds light, all peaceful beginnings of government were founded upon the consent of the people who formed them. I say peaceful because elsewhere I shall discuss conquest, which some regard as another way governments begin.
The other objection raised against political societies beginning in the way I have described is as follows:
Since everyone is born under some existing government, nobody can ever be free to unite with others and establish a new one, or ever have the power to create a lawful government.

If this argument is sound, I ask how so many lawful monarchies came into existence. On that assumption, show me one man in any age free to establish a lawful monarchy, and I undertake to show you ten others equally free at the same time to unite and establish a new government, monarchical or otherwise. It is demonstrable that if one person born under another's dominion can be free enough to command others in a new and separate empire, everyone born under another's dominion can be equally free. Each may become a ruler or subject of a distinct government. By their own principle, therefore, either everyone is free, whatever the circumstances of birth, or only one lawful prince and government exist in the world. They then need only show us which it is. Once they do, I have no doubt that all humanity will readily agree to obey him.

It sufficiently answers their objection to show that it involves its own advocates in the same difficulties they raise against others. Yet I shall examine its weakness a little further. Everyone, they say, is born under government and therefore cannot be free to begin another. Everyone is born subject to a father or prince and so remains perpetually bound in subjection and allegiance. Plainly, however, humanity has never acknowledged or accepted any such natural subjection at birth, whether to father or prince, binding people without their consent to those rulers and their heirs.

No historical examples, sacred or secular, occur more frequently than people withdrawing themselves and their obedience from the jurisdiction of their birth and the family or community that raised them, then going to other places and establishing new governments of their own there. This produced the many small commonwealths of the earliest ages. They multiplied wherever room remained, until stronger or more fortunate states swallowed weaker ones; the great states in turn broke apart into smaller dominions. Every example testifies against paternal sovereignty and plainly proves that governments did not originally arise from a father's natural right descending to his heirs. On that basis, so many little kingdoms could not have existed. There could only have been one universal monarchy, unless people were free to leave their families and whatever government had been established within them and create distinct commonwealths or other governments as they chose.

This has been the world's practice from the beginning to the present. The freedom of humanity is no more obstructed today by birth under ancient, established political societies, with their settled laws and fixed forms of government, than it would be by birth in the woods among the unrestricted inhabitants who roam freely there. Those who claim that birth under a government naturally makes us its subjects, removing every claim to the freedom of the state of nature, offer only one reason apart from paternal power, which we have already answered. They say our fathers or ancestors surrendered their natural liberty and thereby bound themselves and their descendants perpetually to the government they accepted. Certainly, a person is bound by the commitments and promises he makes for himself. But no agreement whatsoever can bind his children or descendants. Once grown, his son is as free as the father; the father's acts can no more surrender the son's liberty than anyone else's. He may indeed attach conditions to land he enjoyed as a commonwealth's subject, requiring his son to join that community if he wants those possessions. The estate belongs to the father, who may dispose of or settle it as he pleases.

This has generally caused the misunderstanding. Commonwealths neither allow parts of their territory to be detached nor allow outsiders to enjoy them. A son therefore ordinarily receives his father's possessions only on the same terms, becoming a member of the society. He immediately places himself under its established government, as fully as any other subject. Free people born under government give the consent that alone makes them members separately, each in turn on reaching adulthood, rather than all together in a crowd. People therefore overlook it. Assuming consent was never given, or is unnecessary, they conclude that people are naturally subjects simply because they are human.

Yet governments themselves plainly understand otherwise. They claim no power over a son merely because they possessed power over his father, and do not regard children as subjects merely because their fathers were. If an English subject has a child with an English woman in France, whose subject is that child? Not the king of England's, since admission to those privileges requires permission. Not the king of France's, since otherwise how could the father freely take him away and raise him as he chooses? Who has ever been judged a traitor or deserter for leaving or fighting against a country merely because he was born there to foreign parents? Both governments' own practice and sound reason therefore show that a child is born subject to no country or government. He remains under his father's care and authority until the age of discretion. Then he is free to choose the government and body politic he will join. If an Englishman's son born in France enjoys this liberty, his father's subjection to this kingdom plainly does not bind him, nor does any ancestral agreement. Why should the same man's son lack that liberty merely because he was born elsewhere? A father's natural power over his children is identical wherever their birth occurs, and natural obligations are not confined by the artificial boundaries of kingdoms and commonwealths.

As already shown, every person is naturally free, and nothing except his own consent can subject him to any earthly power. We must therefore consider what should count as a sufficient declaration of a person's consent to make him subject to a government's laws. The familiar distinction between express and tacit consent concerns our present question. Nobody doubts that someone entering a society through express consent becomes its full member and a subject of that government. The difficulty is deciding what should count as tacit consent and how far it binds him. In other words, how far should someone who has made no declaration at all be regarded as having consented and thereby submitted to a government? My answer is that anyone possessing or enjoying any part of a government's territory thereby gives tacit consent. During the whole period of that enjoyment, he is obliged to obey its laws as fully as anyone living under them. This applies whether he owns land for himself and his heirs forever, rents a lodging for only a week, or merely travels freely along the highway. In effect, the obligation extends to anyone's very presence within the territory of that government.

To understand this better, consider what a person does when he first incorporates himself into a commonwealth. In joining it, he also attaches and submits to the community whatever possessions he already has or later acquires that do not already belong to another government. It would be a direct contradiction to enter society with others for the security and regulation of property while supposing one's own land exempt from the jurisdiction of that government. The society's laws are to regulate ownership of that land, and its proprietor is himself a subject of the government. Therefore, through the same act that joins his previously free person to a commonwealth, he also joins his previously free possessions to it. Both person and possessions become subject to the government and dominion of that commonwealth for as long as it exists. Anyone who afterwards enjoys any part of the land attached to and governed by it—through inheritance, purchase, permission, or otherwise—must accept the condition already attached to that land. He must submit to the government of the commonwealth under whose jurisdiction it lies, as fully as any of its subjects.

But government's direct jurisdiction covers only the land. Before the possessor has actually incorporated himself into the society, government reaches him only insofar as he lives on that land and enjoys its possession. The obligation to submit that arises from such enjoyment therefore begins when the enjoyment begins and ends when it ends. Whenever an owner who has given only tacit consent gives up possession by donation, sale, or otherwise, he is free to leave and incorporate himself into another commonwealth. He may also agree with others to establish a new one in vacuis locis, in any part of the world where they find free, unoccupied land. By contrast, anyone who has once consented to membership of a commonwealth through an actual agreement and an express declaration is perpetually and indispensably bound to remain its subject. He can never return to the liberty of the state of nature unless some calamity dissolves the government he lived under, or a public act cuts him off from further membership.

Submitting to a country's laws, living peacefully, and enjoying their privileges and protection do not make someone a member of its society. This is merely local protection on one side and the corresponding obedience on the other, owed to and by everyone who, not being in a state of war, enters territory belonging to a government, throughout every part to which the force of its laws extends. They no more make him a permanent subject or member than temporarily staying in another person's family would make him that person's subject, although during his stay he must follow the household's rules and government. Thus foreigners may spend their entire lives under another government, enjoying its privileges and protection. Although conscience binds them to submit to its administration as fully as any denizen, this does not make them subjects or members of that commonwealth. Only actual entry through a positive undertaking, express promise, and agreement can do so. This is my view of political societies' beginnings and of the consent that makes anyone a member of a commonwealth.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 — Of the Ends of Political Society and Government
paragraphs: If a person in the state of nature is as free as we have said—absolute master of his own person and possessions, equal to the greatest and subject to nobody—why would he surrender that freedom? Why give up this dominion and submit to another power's rule and control? The answer is obvious. Although he has that right in the state of nature, his enjoyment of it is very uncertain and constantly vulnerable to others' attacks. Everyone is as much a king as he is, everyone his equal, and most do not strictly observe fairness and justice. His enjoyment of property is therefore very unsafe and insecure. This makes him willing to leave a condition that, however free, is full of fear and constant danger. With good reason he seeks and willingly joins others already united, or wishing to unite, for the mutual preservation of their lives, liberties, and estates. I give these the general name of property.

The great and principal purpose for which people unite in commonwealths and place themselves under government is therefore the preservation of their property. The state of nature lacks many things needed for that purpose.

First, it lacks an established, settled, known law accepted by common consent as the standard of right and wrong and the common measure for deciding every dispute. Although the law of nature is clear and intelligible to every rational creature, people are biased by their own interests and ignorant through failure to study it. They are therefore reluctant to acknowledge it as binding law when it must be applied to their own particular cases.

Second, the state of nature lacks a recognized and impartial judge authorized to settle every dispute under established law. Everyone there judges and executes the law of nature himself. Because people favour themselves, passion and revenge readily carry them too far and make them too heated in their own cases. Negligence and lack of concern make them equally likely to do too little in other people's cases.

Third, the state of nature often lacks power to support a just sentence and ensure its proper execution. Wrongdoers seldom fail to use force to maintain their injustice whenever they can. Such resistance often makes punishment dangerous, and frequently destructive, for those who attempt to carry it out.

Thus, despite all the privileges of the state of nature, people remain in a poor condition while living in it and are quickly driven into society. This explains why we seldom find groups living together in that condition for long. Each person's irregular and uncertain exercise of the power to punish others' offences exposes them to difficulties. They take refuge under established governmental laws and seek there the preservation of their property. That is why they so willingly surrender their individual powers of punishment, leaving them to those appointed from among them, acting by rules agreed on by the community or its authorized representatives. Here we find both the original right and the origin of legislative and executive power, as well as of governments and societies themselves.
For in the state of nature, apart from his freedom to enjoy innocent pleasures, a person has two powers.

The first is to do whatever he considers appropriate to preserve himself and others within the permissions of the law of nature. Through that law, common to everyone, he and the rest of humanity form one community, one society distinct from all other creatures. Were it not for the corruption and viciousness of degenerate people, no other society would be needed. People would have no need to leave this great natural community and form smaller, separate associations through express agreements.

The other power someone possesses in the state of nature is the power to punish crimes against that law. He gives up both powers when he joins what I may call a private or particular political society, incorporating himself into a commonwealth separate from the rest of humanity.

He surrenders the first power—the freedom to do whatever he thought necessary for preserving himself and the rest of humanity—to regulation by the society's laws, as far as his preservation and that of the other members require. In many respects, these laws restrict the liberty he previously enjoyed under the law of nature.

Second, he gives up the power of punishment altogether. He commits his natural strength, which he previously could use on his own authority to execute the law of nature as he judged appropriate, to assisting society's executive power as its laws require. He now lives in a new condition, enjoying many advantages from the labour, assistance, and company of others in the same community, as well as protection from its combined strength. In providing for himself, he must therefore surrender as much natural liberty as society's good, prosperity, and safety demand. This is not merely necessary but just, since every other member does the same.

On entering society, people hand over the equality, liberty, and executive power they possessed in the state of nature, allowing the legislative to direct them as society's good requires. Yet everyone does this solely to better preserve himself, his liberty, and his property: no rational creature can be supposed to change his condition with the intention of making it worse. The society's power, or that of the legislative it establishes, can therefore never extend beyond the common good. It must secure everyone's property by remedying the three defects already described, which made the state of nature so unsafe and uncomfortable. Whoever holds a commonwealth's legislative or supreme power must consequently govern by established, standing laws, made public and known to the people, rather than by improvised decrees. Impartial and honest judges must settle disputes according to those laws. The community's force may be used at home only to execute them, and abroad to prevent or remedy foreign injuries and protect the community against incursions and invasion. All of this must serve no purpose except the people's peace, safety, and public good.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 — Of the Forms of a Commonwealth
paragraphs: THE majority — having, as has been shown, upon men’s first uniting into society, the whole power of the community naturally in them — may employ all that power in making laws for the community from time to time, and in executing those laws by officers of their own appointing. And then the form of government is a perfect democracy. Or else they may put the power of making laws into the hands of a few select men, and their heirs or successors — and then it is an oligarchy. Or else into the hands of one man — and then it is a monarchy. If to him and his heirs, it is a hereditary monarchy. If to him only for life, but upon his death the power of nominating a successor returning to them, it is an elective monarchy. And accordingly, the community may make compound and mixed forms of government from these, as they think good. And if the legislative power is at first given by the majority to one or more persons only for their lives, or for any limited time, with the supreme power then to revert to them again — when it is so reverted, the community may dispose of it again anew into whatever hands they please, and so constitute a new form of government. For the form of government depending on the placing of the supreme power, which is the legislative — it being impossible to conceive that an inferior power should prescribe to a superior, or that any but the supreme should make laws — according as the power of making laws is placed, such is the form of the commonwealth.

By “commonwealth” I must be understood all along to mean not a democracy, or any particular form of government, but any independent community — what the Latins signified by the word civitas. The word which best answers to it in our language is “commonwealth,” and most properly expresses such a society of men, which “community” or “city” in English does not. For there may be subordinate communities in a government; and “city” among us has a quite different notion from “commonwealth.” And therefore, to avoid ambiguity, I crave leave to use the word “commonwealth” in the sense in which I find it used by king James the first; and I take it to be its genuine meaning. If anybody dislikes it, I consent with him to change it for a bet

chapters.title: Chapter 11 — Of the Extent of the Legislative Power
paragraphs: People's great purpose in entering society is to enjoy their property peacefully and safely, and society's established laws are the chief means of doing so. The first and fundamental positive law of every commonwealth therefore establishes the legislative power. The first and fundamental natural law, governing even the legislative itself, is the preservation of society and, as far as the public good permits, every person within it. The legislative is not merely the commonwealth's supreme power: it is sacred and unalterable in the hands where the community has placed it. No other body's decree, whatever its form or the force behind it, can have the authority and binding force of law without approval from the legislative chosen and appointed by the public. Without this, it lacks what is absolutely necessary to make it law:* the society's consent. Nobody can legislate for that society except by its own consent and authority derived from it. All obedience anyone may owe through the most solemn obligations therefore ultimately rests with this supreme power and is directed by its laws. No oath to any foreign power or subordinate domestic authority can release a member from obedience to a legislative acting within its trust. Nor can such an oath require obedience contrary to enacted laws or beyond what they allow. Imagining someone ultimately bound to obey a power within society other than the supreme power is ridiculous.

(*“The lawful power to make laws commanding entire political societies belongs so properly to those whole societies that any prince or potentate on earth who exercises it on his own, without an express commission received immediately and personally from God, or authority originally derived from the consent of those on whom he imposes laws, commits nothing better than tyranny. Therefore, enactments that public approval has not made laws are not laws.” Hooker’s Eccl. Pol. l. i. sect. 10.

“On this point we must observe that such men naturally possess no full and complete power to command entire political multitudes. Without our consent, therefore, no living person could command us in that way. We consent to be commanded when the society of which we form a part has previously consented, without afterwards revoking that consent through an equally universal agreement. Human laws of every kind therefore have force through consent.” Ibid.)

Although the legislative is the supreme power in every commonwealth, whether held by one person or several, and whether continuously existing or meeting only at intervals, it nevertheless has these limits:

First, it does not and cannot possess absolutely arbitrary power over people's lives and fortunes. It consists only of each member's combined power surrendered to the person or assembly that legislates. It cannot exceed the power those people possessed in the state of nature before entering society and surrendering it to the community. Nobody can transfer more power than he himself possesses, and nobody has absolute, arbitrary power over himself or anyone else to destroy his own life or take another's life or property. As proved, a person cannot subject himself to someone else's arbitrary power. In the state of nature he had no arbitrary authority over another's life, liberty, or possessions, but only the authority the law of nature allowed for preserving himself and humanity. This is all he does, or can, surrender to the commonwealth and through it to the legislative. The legislative can therefore possess no more. Even at its furthest extent, its power is limited to society's public good. Preservation is its only purpose, so it can never have a right to destroy, enslave, or deliberately impoverish its subjects.* The obligations of the law of nature do not end in society. In many cases they become stronger, with known penalties attached by human laws to enforce compliance. The law of nature thus remains an eternal rule for everyone, legislators included. The rules they make for others' actions, like their own and everyone else's actions, must conform to the law of nature—that is, God's will, which it declares. Since nature's fundamental law is humanity's preservation, no human enactment contrary to it can be good or valid.

(*“Two foundations support public societies. One is the natural inclination through which everyone desires social life and fellowship. The other is an arrangement, expressly or tacitly agreed upon, concerning the manner of their union in living together. We call this latter the law of a commonwealth: the very soul of a political body, whose parts the law animates, holds together, and sets to work in actions the common good requires. Political laws, established for outward order and government among people, are never properly framed unless they assume that the human will is inwardly stubborn, rebellious, and resistant to obedience to nature's sacred laws. In short, they must assume that, through his depraved mind, man is little better than a wild beast. They must nevertheless arrange his outward actions so that these do not obstruct the common good for which societies are founded. Unless they do this, the laws are imperfect.” Hooker’s Eccl. Pol. l. i. sect. 10.)

Second, the legislative or supreme authority cannot claim power to rule through arbitrary decrees improvised for the occasion. It remains bound to administer justice and determine the rights of its subjects through established, published standing laws and recognized judges duly authorized to apply them.* The law of nature is unwritten and exists nowhere except in people's minds. Without an established judge, someone who misquotes or misapplies it through passion or self-interest cannot easily be convinced of his mistake. It therefore fails properly to determine rights and protect property, especially when everyone judges, interprets, and executes it in his own case. Moreover, someone in the right usually has only his individual strength, insufficient to defend himself against injury or punish offenders. To avoid these difficulties, which disturb property in the state of nature, people unite in societies. They want society's combined strength to secure and defend their property, with standing rules defining its boundaries so everyone knows what belongs to him. For this purpose they surrender all their natural power to the society they join. The community places legislative authority in whichever hands it chooses, on the trust that declared laws will govern its members. Otherwise their peace, security, and property would remain as uncertain as in the state of nature.

(*“Human laws are standards for the people whose actions they must direct. Yet these standards themselves have higher rules by which they must be measured: the law of God and the law of nature. Human laws must therefore be made according to nature's general laws and without contradicting any positive law of scripture; otherwise they are badly made.” Hooker’s Eccl. Pol. l. iii. sect. 9.
“Compelling people to anything inconvenient seems unreasonable.” Ibid. l. i. sect. 10.)

Neither absolute arbitrary power nor government without settled, standing laws is consistent with society's and government's purposes. People would not surrender the freedom of the state of nature and bind themselves under government unless doing so preserved their lives, liberties, and fortunes, securing peace and quiet through established rules of right and property. Even if they had the power, we cannot suppose they intended to give one or more people absolute, arbitrary authority over their persons and estates, arming the magistrate to impose his unlimited will upon them. This would make them worse off than in the state of nature. There they could defend their rights against injury and stood on equal terms of force, whether threatened by one person or several acting together. But by supposedly surrendering to a legislator's absolute, arbitrary will and power, they disarm themselves and arm him to prey on them whenever he chooses. Someone exposed to one man's arbitrary power when that man commands 100,000 is far worse off than someone exposed to 100,000 separate men's arbitrary powers. Nobody can guarantee that the commander's will is better than other people's, though his force is 100,000 times greater. Whatever the commonwealth's form, its rulers must therefore govern through declared and accepted laws rather than improvised dictates and unsettled decisions. People would otherwise be far worse off than in the state of nature: they would have armed one or a few with the combined power of a multitude, allowing them to compel obedience at pleasure to excessive, unlimited decrees arising from sudden thoughts or unrestricted wills unknown until that moment. No established standards would remain to guide and justify people's actions. Since government's entire power exists only for society's good, it must neither be arbitrary nor exercised at pleasure. Established and published laws must govern its exercise, allowing people to know their duties and live safely within the law's bounds. Rulers too must remain within limits, without the temptation to use their power for purposes or by methods they would conceal or reluctantly acknowledge.
