Third, the supreme power cannot take any part of a person's property without his own consent. The preservation of property is the very purpose of government, and the purpose for which people leave their previous condition and enter into society together. This necessarily assumes and requires that people possess property. Otherwise joining society would deprive them of the very thing they joined to preserve—an absurdity too gross for anyone to admit. Since members of society possess property, their right to goods made theirs by community law means nobody may take their wealth or any portion of it without their consent. Without that, they have no property at all: I do not truly own something another can rightfully take whenever he pleases against my consent. It is therefore mistaken to suppose a commonwealth's supreme or legislative power can do whatever it wishes, dispose arbitrarily of subjects' estates, or take any portion at pleasure. This is less to be feared where the legislative consists wholly or partly of changing assemblies whose members, after dissolution, return to equal subjection with everyone else under their country's ordinary laws. But where legislative power belongs to a permanent assembly or one man, as in absolute monarchies, the danger remains that rulers will consider their interests separate from the community's. They may then enlarge their wealth and power by taking whatever they choose from the people. A person's property is not secure merely because fair laws define its boundaries between him and fellow subjects, if their ruler can take whatever portion he likes from any private person and use or dispose of it as he chooses.

Government, whoever holds it, is entrusted, as I have shown, on the condition and for the purpose that people may possess and secure their property. A prince or senate may possess the power to make laws regulating the property of subjects in their dealings with one another. Yet they can never have power to take for themselves the whole or any portion of a subject's property without that person's own consent. That would effectively leave him with no property at all. Ordinary military discipline shows that even necessary absolute power is not arbitrary merely because absolute. It remains limited by the reason and purposes that make it absolute in particular cases. Preserving the army, and through it the entire commonwealth, requires absolute obedience to every superior officer's orders. Disobeying or disputing even the most dangerous or unreasonable order is rightly punishable by death. Yet a serjeant who can command a soldier to march towards a cannon's mouth or stand in a breach where death is almost certain cannot command him to hand over one penny. A general may condemn him to death for deserting his post or refusing the most desperate orders. But all that absolute power over life and death cannot dispose of one farthing of his estate or seize the smallest portion of his goods, although the general may command any action and hang him for the slightest disobedience. Such blind obedience is necessary for the commander's purpose: preserving the rest. Disposing of the soldier's goods has nothing to do with it.

Governments admittedly cost a great deal to maintain, and everyone enjoying a share of their protection should contribute a proportionate amount from his estate. Yet the contribution must still be made with his own consent: that is, with the consent of the majority, expressed either by the people themselves or through representatives whom they have chosen for that purpose. Anyone claiming authority to impose and collect taxes by his own power, without such public consent, invades the fundamental law of property and overturns government's purpose. For what property do I possess in something another may rightfully take for himself whenever he pleases?

Fourth, the legislative cannot hand the lawmaking power to anyone else. Its authority is delegated by the people, and those receiving it cannot pass it onwards. Only the people themselves may determine the form of their commonwealth by establishing its legislative and choosing who holds it. Once they have said that they will submit to rules and laws made by specified people in specified forms, nobody else can declare that different people will legislate for them. Nor can they be bound by laws except those enacted by the people they chose and authorized to make them. Legislative power derives from an express, voluntary public grant and institution, and cannot exceed what that grant conveyed. The grant authorizes making laws, not making legislators. The legislative therefore has no power to transfer its lawmaking authority into other hands.
These are the limits imposed on every commonwealth's legislative power, whatever its form of government, by the trust society places in it and by the law of God and nature.

First, legislators must govern through published, established laws that do not change to suit particular cases. The same rule must apply to rich and poor, to the favourite at court and the countryman at his plough.
Second, these laws must ultimately be designed for no purpose other than the good of the people.

Third, they must not tax people's property without the people's consent, given personally or through deputies. This properly concerns only governments where the legislative exists continuously, or at least where the people have not reserved any part of legislative power to deputies whom they themselves elect from time to time.
Fourth, the legislative must not and cannot transfer lawmaking power to anyone else, or place it anywhere except where the people have placed it.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 — Of the Legislative, Executive, and Federative Power of the Commonwealth
paragraphs: Legislative power has the right to direct how the commonwealth's force is to be employed for the preservation of the community and all its members. Yet laws that must be constantly executed, and whose force must continue without interruption, can themselves be made within a short time. The legislative therefore need not remain continuously in existence, since it does not always have business to perform. Moreover, human weakness, always inclined to grasp at power, may be too greatly tempted if the very same people who make the laws also hold the power to execute them. They could exempt themselves from obedience to their own laws and shape both the making and execution of law to their private advantage. They would thereby acquire interests distinct from those of the rest of the community, contrary to society's and government's purpose. In well-ordered commonwealths, where the good of the whole receives its proper consideration, legislative power therefore belongs to several people who, duly assembled, make laws either alone or jointly with others. Once they have done so, they separate again and become subject to the laws they made. This provides an additional, immediate obligation to ensure that those laws serve the public good.

But laws made together in a short time retain a constant and lasting force. They require continual execution, or continual attention to that task. There must therefore always be an existing power responsible for executing the laws that have been made and remain in force. This is why legislative and executive power are often separated.

Every commonwealth also possesses another power we may call natural, because it corresponds to the power everyone naturally had before entering society. Within a commonwealth, members remain distinct individuals in relation to one another and are governed as such by society's laws. In relation to the rest of humanity, however, they form one body, which remains in the state of nature with outsiders just as each member previously did. Disputes between a member and outsiders are therefore handled by the public, and an injury to one member commits the whole body to seeking redress. Considered in this respect, therefore, the whole community forms one single body in the state of nature with respect to all other states and every person outside that community.

This includes power over war and peace, leagues and alliances, and all dealings with people and communities outside the commonwealth. It may be called federative if anyone wishes. Provided the thing itself is understood, I am indifferent to its name.

These two powers, executive and federative, are genuinely distinct from one another. The executive concerns the execution of society's domestic laws within the society itself, upon everyone who belongs to it. The federative concerns management of the public's security and interests abroad, in dealings with all those from whom the community might receive either benefit or harm. Nevertheless, the two are almost always united. Good or bad management of federative power matters greatly to a commonwealth, but it is much less readily directed by pre-existing, standing, positive laws than executive power. It must therefore be entrusted to its holders' prudence and wisdom, to be used for the public good. Laws concerning relations between subjects can properly precede the actions they direct. But dealings with foreigners depend greatly on those foreigners' actions and on changing plans and interests. They must therefore be left largely to the discretion of those entrusted with this power, who must use their best judgment for the commonwealth's advantage.

Although, as I said, executive and federative powers are genuinely distinct, they can hardly be separated and simultaneously entrusted to different people. Both require society's force for their exercise. Placing the commonwealth's force in separate hands not subordinate to one another is almost impracticable. If executive and federative power belonged to people able to act independently, public force would fall under different commands. Such an arrangement would be likely, at some time or other, to produce disorder and eventually ruin.

chapters.title: Chapter 13 — Of the Subordination of the Powers of the Commonwealth
paragraphs: In an established commonwealth standing on its own foundations and acting according to its nature—that is, preserving the community—there can be only one supreme power, the legislative. Every other power is and must be subordinate to it. Yet the legislative holds its power only in trust for particular purposes. The people therefore retain supreme power to remove or alter it when it acts against that trust. Every power entrusted for a purpose is limited by that purpose. When the purpose is plainly neglected or opposed, the trust is necessarily forfeited and power returns to those who granted it. They may place it wherever they now judge best for their safety and security. Thus the community always retains supreme power to save itself from anyone's schemes, even its own legislators', if they become foolish or wicked enough to plot against subjects' liberties and property. Neither an individual nor a society has power to surrender its preservation, or the means of preserving itself, to another's absolute will and arbitrary dominion. Whenever someone tries to reduce them to such slavery, they therefore retain the right to preserve what they have no power to surrender, and to free themselves from those violating the fundamental, sacred, unchangeable law of self-preservation for which they entered society. In this respect the community may be called permanently supreme. But this does not describe its position under an existing form of government, because the people's power cannot operate until that government is dissolved.

In every case, while government continues, the legislative is supreme. Whoever can give laws to another must be his superior. The legislative is society's legislative only because it has the right to make laws for all its parts and every member, prescribing rules of conduct and authorizing execution when those rules are broken. It must therefore be the supreme power. Every other power held by any member or part of society derives from it and remains subordinate to it.

In some commonwealths the legislative does not meet continuously, while executive power belongs to one person who also shares legislative authority. That person may reasonably be called supreme in a particular sense. He does not individually possess all supreme power, which is lawmaking. But he holds supreme executive power, from which lesser magistrates derive all or at least most of their subordinate authorities. Nor does he have a legislative superior: no law can be made without his consent, and he can hardly be expected to consent to subjecting himself to the legislative's other part. In this sense “supreme” is appropriate. Yet oaths of allegiance and fealty are sworn to him not as supreme legislator but as supreme executor of laws made jointly by himself and others. Allegiance means only obedience according to law. When he violates the law, he loses the right to obedience. He can claim it only as a public person invested with the law's power: the image, embodiment, or representative of the commonwealth, moved by society's will as declared in its laws. In that capacity he possesses no will or power except the law's. When he abandons that representation and public will to act by his private will, he lowers himself to an ordinary private person, with no power or will entitled to obedience. Members owe obedience only to society's public will.

Where executive power belongs to anyone who does not also share legislative power, it is plainly subordinate and accountable to the legislative, which may change or remove it at pleasure. Supreme executive power itself is therefore not exempt from subordination. The exemption belongs to an executive who also shares legislative authority and has no separate legislative superior to answer to except insofar as he joins and consents. He is consequently subordinate only as far as he chooses, which we may safely conclude will be very little. We need not discuss the other administrative and subordinate powers of a commonwealth. Their immense variety under different customs and constitutions makes a complete account impossible. For our present purpose, we need observe only that none has any authority beyond what an express grant and commission delegate to it. Every one of them is accountable to some other power within the commonwealth.

A continuously existing legislative is neither necessary nor even convenient. A continuously existing executive is absolutely necessary, because new laws are not always needed, but existing laws always require execution. When the legislative entrusts execution of its laws to other hands, it retains power to reclaim that function whenever it finds cause and to punish administration contrary to law. The same holds for federative power. Both federative and executive powers serve and remain subordinate to the legislative, which, as shown, is supreme in an established commonwealth. Here we suppose the legislative consists of several people. If it belonged to one person, it would necessarily exist continuously, and that supreme person would naturally hold supreme executive as well as legislative power. A legislative assembly may meet and exercise its authority at times set by the original constitution or by its own adjournment. If neither specifies a time and no other method of summoning it is prescribed, it may assemble whenever it wishes. The people placed supreme power in its hands, where that power remains. It may therefore exercise it at pleasure unless the original constitution limits it to particular seasons or it has used its supreme authority to adjourn until a specified time. When that time arrives, it has the right to meet and act again.

If the legislative, or part of it, consists of representatives elected for a particular occasion who afterwards return to ordinary subjecthood and regain a legislative share only through reelection, the people must also exercise this power of choosing their representatives, either at certain appointed seasons or when they are summoned to make that choice. In the latter case, summoning the legislative ordinarily belongs to the executive, subject to one of two arrangements concerning time. The original constitution may require meetings and action at fixed intervals; the executive then merely performs the administrative task of issuing directions for election and assembly in the proper forms. Alternatively, his prudence determines when new elections should summon them, as public circumstances or emergencies require old laws to be amended, new ones made, or existing and threatened difficulties remedied or prevented.

Someone may ask at this point: what if the executive power, possessing the force of the commonwealth, uses that very force to prevent the legislative from meeting and carrying out its work when the original constitution or the urgent needs of the public require it? I answer that using force against the people without authority, contrary to the executive's trust, creates a state of war with them. They have a right to restore their legislative to the exercise of its power. They established it to make laws at specified times or whenever needed. If force prevents this activity, so necessary to society and essential to the people's safety and preservation, they have a right to remove that force by force. In every condition and circumstance, the true remedy for unauthorized force is force in opposition. Whoever uses force without authority always enters a state of war as the aggressor and becomes liable to treatment accordingly.

The power entrusted to the executive to summon and dismiss the legislative does not place the executive above it. It is a trust given him for the people's safety, in a case where human affairs are too uncertain and changeable to admit a steady, fixed rule. The first founders of government could not possibly foresee future events well enough to prescribe appropriate intervals and durations for legislative assemblies for all time to come. No timetable could exactly meet every future need of the commonwealth. The best remedy they could find was to trust the prudence of someone who would always be present and whose business was to watch over the public good. Constantly recurring meetings and unnecessarily lengthy sessions would burden the people, and in time must create still more dangerous difficulties. Yet affairs sometimes change so quickly that the legislative's immediate help is needed. Any delay in summoning it might endanger the public. At other times its business might be so extensive that a fixed sitting would end before its work was done, depriving the public of benefits obtainable only through mature deliberation. With fixed intervals and durations for legislative meetings and action, the community would therefore sooner or later face serious danger on one side or the other. What could prevent this except entrusting the matter to the judgment of someone present, familiar with the condition of public affairs, and able to employ the prerogative for public good? Where could this trust be better placed than in the hands of the person entrusted with executing the laws for that same purpose? Thus, where the original constitution did not settle the times for assembling and sitting, their regulation naturally fell into the executive's hands. It was not arbitrary power depending on his pleasure, but a continuing trust that it would be exercised only for public welfare, as the needs of the times and changes in affairs required. Whether fixed meeting periods, discretion left to the prince to summon the legislative, or perhaps a mixture of both creates the fewest difficulties is not my concern here. I seek only to show that, although the executive may possess the prerogative of summoning and dissolving these legislative assemblies, he is not thereby superior to the legislative itself.

Worldly affairs change so constantly that nothing remains long in the same condition. People, riches, trade, and power all change their locations. Mighty, flourishing cities fall into ruin and eventually become neglected and desolate corners of the world, while places formerly seldom visited develop into populous countries, filled with both inhabitants and wealth. But changes are unequal, and private interests often preserve customs and privileges after their reasons disappear. Consequently, where elected representatives form part of the legislative, representation often becomes over time very unequal and disproportionate to its original justification. We can see the gross absurdity of following custom after reason has abandoned it when a town exists only in name, without even ruins, scarcely containing a sheepfold's worth of buildings or more inhabitants than a shepherd, yet sends as many legislators as an entire populous, wealthy county. Foreigners look on in astonishment at this arrangement, and everyone must admit that it urgently needs a remedy. Most nevertheless think a remedy difficult to find. Establishing the legislative is society's original and supreme act, preceding every positive law and depending entirely on the people; no lesser authority can alter it. Once the legislative is established, the people in the kind of government we are discussing cannot act while that government continues. The defect is therefore considered beyond remedy.

Salus populi suprema lex is certainly so just and fundamental a rule that anyone sincerely following it cannot go dangerously wrong. Suppose the executive, who can summon the legislative, attends to representation's true proportions rather than its customary form. He regulates the number of members from each place entitled to distinct representation by sound reason rather than old custom. No incorporated section of the people can claim that right except in proportion to its contribution to the public. This cannot be judged the creation of a new legislative: it restores the old and true one, correcting disorders introduced gradually and inevitably by time. Fair and equal representation serves both the people's interests and their intentions. Whoever brings representation closest to that standard unquestionably supports and strengthens government and must receive the community's consent and approval. Prerogative is simply the prince's power to provide for public good where unforeseen and uncertain events make fixed, unchangeable laws unsafe guides. Anything plainly done for the people's good and to establish government on its true foundations is, and always will be, rightful prerogative. The power to create new corporations and thus new representatives assumes that representation's measures may change over time. Places previously unrepresented may acquire a just claim, and by the same reasoning places formerly represented may lose that claim by becoming too insignificant for the privilege. A departure from the present arrangement, perhaps itself produced by corruption or decay, does not constitute an attack on government. What does is a tendency to injure or oppress the people, elevating one section or party while subjecting the rest unequally. Whatever must be acknowledged as benefiting society and the people generally through just and lasting measures will justify itself once done. Whenever people choose representatives on just and undeniably equal terms consistent with government's original structure, the choice must be recognized as society's will and act, whoever permitted or caused them to do it.

chapters.title: Chapter 14 — Of Prerogative
paragraphs: Where legislative and executive powers belong to different hands, as they do in all limited monarchies and well-designed governments, society's good requires leaving various matters to the discretion of whoever holds executive power. Legislators cannot foresee everything that might be useful to the community and provide for it through laws. The executor of the laws, already possessing the necessary power, therefore has a right under the common law of nature to use it for society's benefit in many cases where domestic law gives no direction. He may do so until the legislative can conveniently assemble to make provision. Many things cannot possibly be covered by law. They must necessarily be left to the judgment of the person holding executive power, to arrange as public good and advantage require. Indeed, the laws themselves should sometimes yield to executive power—or rather to the fundamental law of nature and government: that all society's members should be preserved as far as possible. Many accidents may arise in which strict and rigid obedience to law would do harm. Refusing to demolish an innocent man's house to stop a fire when the next house is burning is one example. A person may also fall within the reach of a law that makes no distinction between persons because of an action actually deserving reward and pardon. The ruler should therefore have power in many cases to soften the law's severity and pardon some offenders. Government's purpose is to preserve everyone as far as possible, so even the guilty should be spared wherever doing so does not harm the innocent.

Prerogative is the power to act at one's discretion for the public good without the law's direction, and sometimes even against it. In some governments the lawmaking power does not always exist, and its members are usually too numerous and therefore too slow for the speed execution requires. Moreover, no one can foresee and legislate for every accident and necessity affecting the public. Nor can laws be framed that will never cause harm when enforced inflexibly on every occasion and everyone they reach. The executive power is therefore left a measure of discretion to choose and carry out many actions that the laws themselves do not prescribe.

While this power benefits the community and accords with government's trust and purposes, it is unquestioned prerogative. The people are very seldom, if ever, inclined to raise scruples or insist on fine distinctions about this particular matter. They do not investigate prerogative so long as it serves its intended purpose to any tolerable degree: the people's good, rather than anything plainly contrary to it. But if executive and people dispute some claimed prerogative, the tendency of its exercise to benefit or harm the people will readily settle the question.

It is easy to understand that in governments' infancy, when commonwealths scarcely exceeded families in population, they also scarcely exceeded them in number of laws. Governors watched over them for their good like fathers, and government consisted almost entirely of prerogative. A small number of established laws served their purposes, and the ruler's own discretion, attention, and care supplied whatever those laws left unprovided for. But when error or flattery persuaded weak princes to use this power for private purposes instead of public good, the people had to define prerogative through express laws in the areas where it harmed them. Thus they found declared limits necessary in cases that they and their ancestors had left entirely to the wisdom of princes who used their discretion rightly—that is, for their people's good.

Those who say the people encroach on prerogative when they define any part of it through positive laws thoroughly misunderstand government. In doing this, the people have taken away nothing that rightfully belonged to the prince. They have only declared that the power left without defined limits in his hands, or in his ancestors' hands, was entrusted to be exercised for their good. It was never a power they intended him to possess when he used it for another purpose. Government exists for the community's good. Changes tending towards that purpose cannot invade anyone's rights, because nobody in government can possess a right serving any other purpose. Only actions that harm or obstruct public good are encroachments. Those claiming otherwise speak as though a prince had interests distinct from the community's welfare and had not been established to serve it. That notion is the root of almost every evil and disorder in kingly governments. If it were true, the governed would not be rational creatures joining a community for mutual benefit and appointing rulers to protect and promote it. They would be a herd of inferior creatures under a master who keeps and works them for his own pleasure or profit. If people were brutish and irrational enough to enter society on those terms, prerogative might indeed be what some claim: arbitrary power to do things harmful to the people.

But we cannot suppose a free rational creature would subject himself to another for his own harm. Finding a wise and good ruler, he may nevertheless consider it neither necessary nor useful to define precise limits to every power. Prerogative can therefore mean only the people's permission for rulers to choose various actions for public good where the law is silent, sometimes even against its literal wording, and the people's acceptance of those actions afterwards. A good prince who remembers his trust and cares for his people's welfare cannot have too much prerogative—that is, too much power to do good. But a weak and wicked prince may claim as his official right the power predecessors exercised without legal direction, insisting he may use it at pleasure to establish or promote interests separate from the public's. He thereby gives the people reason to assert their rights and limit a power they were content to allow tacitly while it served their good.

Anyone who examines the history of England will therefore find that prerogative was always at its greatest in the hands of our wisest and best princes. Seeing their actions generally directed towards public good, people did not dispute things done for that purpose without legal authority. Human weakness or error might cause small departures—princes are only people, made like others—but their conduct's main direction plainly remained care for the public. Finding reason for satisfaction, the people therefore accepted these princes' actions outside or against the law's literal wording. Without the slightest complaint they allowed prerogative to expand as the princes wished. They rightly judged that their laws suffered no injury, since the princes acted in accordance with the foundation and purpose of every law: the public good.

Princes of this godlike character did indeed possess some claim to arbitrary power under the argument that absolute monarchy is best because God himself governs the universe that way: these kings shared his wisdom and goodness. This explains the saying that good princes' reigns have always been most dangerous to their people's liberties. Their successors, governing with different intentions, turn the good rulers' actions into precedents and measures of their own prerogative. They treat acts done only for public benefit as a right to do harm if they please. Disputes and sometimes public disorders have often followed before people recovered their original rights and secured a declaration that these claims were not prerogative, and never truly had been. Nobody in society can possibly have a right to harm the people. Yet it is entirely possible and reasonable that people would not set limits to the prerogative of rulers who themselves never went beyond the public good's bounds. Prerogative is simply power to do public good without a rule.

In England, deciding the precise time, place, and duration of parliaments is certainly a royal prerogative. But it remains entrusted for the nation's good, to be used as changing circumstances and needs require. It was impossible to foresee which place would always be the most suitable for parliament to assemble, or what season and time would best meet each occasion. Choosing these was therefore left to executive power, to serve public good as effectively as possible and best fulfil parliament's purposes.

In this matter of prerogative, the familiar old question will naturally be asked again: who is to serve as judge of whether this power has been put to a rightful use? I answer that no earthly judge can stand between an existing executive possessing this prerogative and a legislative dependent on his will for assembly. Nor can one stand between the legislative and the people if either legislative or executive, once holding power, plans or attempts to enslave or destroy them. Here, as wherever they lack an earthly judge, the people's only remedy is an appeal to heaven. In such attempts rulers exercise power the people never granted. The people can never be supposed to consent to being governed for their harm, so rulers doing this act without right. Whenever the people as a body, or an individual, lose their rights or suffer the exercise of unauthorized power without earthly appeal, they are free to appeal to heaven when they judge the matter important enough. The people cannot judge in the sense of possessing, under that society's constitution, a superior authority to decide the case and enforce a sentence. Nevertheless, by a law preceding and overriding every human positive law, they retain the ultimate judgment belonging to all humanity where no earthly appeal exists: whether they have just cause to appeal to heaven. They cannot surrender that judgment. Nobody can submit to another so completely as to authorize his own destruction. God and nature never permit him to abandon himself and neglect his preservation. Since he cannot take his own life, neither can he empower another to take it. Nobody should imagine that this creates a perpetual source of disorder. It operates only when the difficulty becomes so great that the majority feel it, grow weary of it, and find correction necessary. An executive, or wise princes, need never expose themselves to this danger. Above everything else they must avoid it, because nothing is more perilous.

chapters.title: Chapter 15 — Of Paternal, Political, and Despotical Power, Considered Together
paragraphs: Although I have already discussed these powers separately, the recent serious mistakes about government seem to have arisen from confusing them with one another. It may therefore be useful to consider them together here.

First, paternal or parental power is simply parents' power to govern their children for the children's good until they acquire reason, or enough knowledge to be considered capable of understanding the rule by which they must govern themselves. That rule may be the law of nature or their country's civil law. They must, I say, be capable of knowing it as well as others living freely under it. God implanted affection and tenderness towards children in parents' hearts, plainly showing that this government was intended not as harsh, arbitrary rule but as assistance, instruction, and preservation of their offspring. However things turn out, as I have proved, there is no reason to suppose parents ever acquire more power over their children's lives and deaths than over anyone else's. Nor can parental power justify keeping an adult child subject to his parents' will beyond the lifelong respect, honour, gratitude, assistance, and support owed to both father and mother for life and education received. Paternal government is indeed natural, then, but it does not extend to political government's purposes or jurisdiction. A father's power does not reach his child's property at all; that property remains entirely and solely at the child's own disposal.

Second, political power is the power everyone possessed in the state of nature and has surrendered to society, and through it to the governors society appoints. The express or tacit trust is that it will serve the members' good and preserve their property. In the state of nature this power, surrendered wherever society can provide security, consists in using whatever means nature permits and a person judges suitable to preserve his property. It also includes punishing others' breaches of the law of nature in whatever way his best reasoning judges most conducive to preserving himself and humanity. In individual hands in the state of nature, its purpose and measure were the preservation of everyone in his society—that is, humanity generally. In the magistrate's hands, it can have no other purpose or measure than preserving society's members in their lives, liberties, and possessions. It therefore cannot be absolute, arbitrary power over lives and fortunes, which must be preserved as far as possible. It is power to make laws and attach penalties tending to preserve the whole by removing only those parts so corrupt that they threaten the sound and healthy. Without that threat, no severity is lawful. The only origin of this political power is a compact and an agreement, made through the mutual consent of all those people who together form the community.

Third, despotical power is the absolute, arbitrary power one person holds over another to take his life whenever he chooses. Nature does not grant this power, having made no such distinction between people. Nor can agreement transfer it, because a person lacking arbitrary power over his own life cannot grant it to someone else. It results only from an aggressor's forfeiture of his life when he enters a state of war with another. He has abandoned reason, which God gave as the rule between people and the common bond uniting humanity in one fellowship and society. Renouncing the peaceful course reason teaches, he uses war's force to impose unjust purposes on another where he has no right. By making force his standard of right, he deserts his own kind for the beasts' kind. He becomes liable to destruction by the injured person and anyone joining in the execution of justice, like any wild beast or harmful brute with which humanity can enjoy neither society nor security.* Thus only captives taken in a just and lawful war are subject to despotical power. It does not arise from agreement and cannot admit any agreement: it is simply a continued state of war. What agreement can be made with someone who is not master of his own life? What condition can he fulfil? Once he is allowed mastery over his own life, his master's despotical, arbitrary power ends. Whoever owns himself and his life also has a right to the means of preserving it. As soon as agreement enters, therefore, slavery ends. Whoever makes terms with his captive gives up absolute power to that extent and ends the state of war.
(*Another copy corrected by Mr. Locke gives the wording as follows: “Noxious brute that is destructive to their being.”)

Nature grants the first power, paternal power, to parents for their children's benefit during minority, compensating for their inability and lack of understanding in managing their property. Here, as elsewhere, property includes what people own in their persons as well as in their goods. Voluntary agreement grants the second, political power, to governors for their subjects' benefit, securing possession and use of their property. Forfeiture grants the third, despotical power, to masters for the masters' own benefit, over those stripped of all property.

Anyone considering these powers' distinct origins, extent, and purposes will see plainly that paternal power falls as far short of a magistrate's power as despotical power exceeds it. Absolute dominion, wherever placed, is not a kind of civil society; it is as incompatible with civil society as slavery is with property. Paternal power exists only where minority prevents a child from managing his property. Political power exists where people have property at their own disposal. Despotical power exists over those who have no property at all.

chapters.title: Chapter 16 — Of Conquest
paragraphs: Governments can originally arise only in the way already described, and political societies can rest only on the people's consent. Yet ambition has filled the world with such disorder that, amid the noise of war occupying so much of human history, that consent receives little attention. Many have therefore mistaken armed force for the people's consent and counted conquest among the origins of government. But conquest is as far from establishing government as demolishing a house is from building a new one in its place. By destroying an earlier commonwealth it often clears the way for a new arrangement, but without the people's consent it can never establish one.

Everyone who refuses to grant robbers and pirates dominion over anyone they can overpower, or to regard promises extorted by unlawful force as binding, will readily agree that an aggressor gains no right over the conquered through an unjust war. He has placed himself in a state of war by unjustly invading another's rights. Suppose a robber breaks into my house and, holding a dagger to my throat, makes me sign deeds transferring my estate to him. Does that give him title? An unjust conqueror forcing my submission with his sword has precisely that title. The injury and crime are identical whether committed by someone wearing a crown or a petty villain. The offender's rank and number of followers make no difference except perhaps to aggravate the offence. The only difference is that great robbers punish lesser ones to keep them obedient, while receiving laurels and triumphs themselves. They are too powerful for worldly justice's weak hands and possess the very force that should punish wrongdoers. What remedy have I against the robber who entered my house? I appeal to law for justice. But perhaps justice is refused; perhaps injury prevents me moving, or robbery leaves me without the means. If God removes every means of remedy, only patience remains. Yet my son, when able, may seek the legal relief denied me. He or his son may renew the appeal until the right is recovered. Suppose the conquered and their children have no earthly court or arbitrator to appeal to. They may then appeal to heaven, as Jephtha did, and repeat that appeal until they regain their ancestors' original right: a legislative approved and freely accepted by the majority. If someone objects that this causes endless trouble, I answer: no more than justice does when open to every appellant. A court punishes someone who needlessly troubles his neighbour. Whoever appeals to heaven must be sure both that he is right and that the right merits the trouble and cost of the appeal. He must answer before a tribunal that cannot be deceived and will repay everyone according to the harm done to fellow subjects—that is, any part of humanity. Plainly, then, conquest in an unjust war confers no claim to the conquered people's subjection or obedience.
But suppose victory favours the rightful side. Let us consider someone conquering in a lawful war and examine what power he acquires and over whom he acquires it.

First, conquest plainly gives him no power over those who conquered alongside him. Those who fought on his side cannot be made worse off by the conquest they helped to achieve; they must remain at least as fully free as they were before the war began. They usually enter his service on agreed terms, expecting to share the spoils and other advantages of victory with their leader, or at least receive some of the conquered territory. I hope the conquering people do not become slaves through conquest, wearing laurels merely to show they are sacrifices to their leader's triumph. Those who base absolute monarchy on the sword's title turn its heroic founders into outright Draw-can-sirs. They forget the officers and soldiers who fought beside them, helped subdue countries, and shared their possession. Some tell us England's monarchy rests on the Norman conquest, giving our princes absolute dominion. Even if that were true, contrary to history, and William had a right to wage war on this island, his dominion by conquest could extend only to the Saxons and Britons then inhabiting it. The Normans who came with him and helped conquer, and all their descendants, remain free, not subjects by conquest, whatever dominion conquest may confer. If I or anyone else claims freedom through descent from them, proving otherwise will be very difficult. The law, making no distinction between the two populations, plainly intends no difference in their freedom or privileges.

Suppose, however, that conquerors and conquered never unite as one people under the same laws and freedom, although this seldom happens. What power does a lawful conqueror then have over those subdued? I say it is purely despotical. He has absolute power over the lives forfeited through unjust war, but not over the lives or fortunes of those who took no part, nor even over the possessions of those who actually fought.

Second, I say the conqueror acquires power only over people who actually assisted, joined, or consented to the unjust force used against him. The people never gave their governors power to commit injustice, including an unjust war, because they never possessed such power themselves. They cannot therefore be charged with the violence and injustice of that war beyond their actual participation in it. They are no more guilty of it than of violence or oppression their governors inflict upon themselves or fellow subjects: they authorized neither. Conquerors seldom bother with this distinction and willingly let war's confusion sweep everyone together. Yet this does not alter what is right. The conqueror's power over lives arises only because those people used force to commit or maintain injustice. It therefore extends only to participants in that force. All the rest remain innocent. He has no more title over those inhabitants of the conquered country who have done him no injury and have therefore made no forfeiture of their lives than he has over any other people who, without injuring or provoking him in any way, have continued to live on fair terms with him.

Third, a conqueror's power over those he defeats in a just war is entirely despotical. He has absolute power over lives forfeited by entering a state of war, but gains no corresponding right or title to their possessions. I have no doubt that this doctrine will seem strange at first sight, since it runs so directly against the familiar practice of the world. In discussing dominion over a country, nothing is more usual than saying someone conquered it, as though conquest automatically conveyed ownership. Yet we should remember that the practice of the strong and powerful, however universal, seldom supplies the rule of right. Part of the conquered people's subjection may indeed consist in being unable to challenge conditions imposed by the conquering sword.

War usually combines force with damage, and an aggressor attacking people seldom avoids harming their estates. Yet force alone places someone in a state of war. He may begin the injury forcibly, or he may first commit it quietly through fraud and then refuse reparation, using force to maintain it. The latter amounts to committing the original injury by force. In either case, the unjust use of force creates war. Someone who breaks into my house and violently expels me does effectively the same thing as someone who enters peacefully and then forcibly excludes me. All this assumes that we are in a condition where no common judge exists on earth to whom I may appeal for a decision and to whose authority we are both obliged to submit. It is of people in this situation that I am now speaking. Unjust force, then, places someone in a state of war with another and causes the guilty person to forfeit his life. He abandons reason, the rule given for relations between people, and adopts force, the beasts' method. The person attacked may therefore destroy him like any savage, ravenous beast threatening his existence.

But a father's wrongdoing is not his children's fault. They may be rational and peaceful despite his brutality and injustice. Through his misconduct and violence he can forfeit only his own life, without involving his children in his guilt or destruction. Nature seeks humanity's preservation as far as possible and gives children a claim to his goods to prevent their perishing. Those goods therefore continue to belong to them. If infancy, absence, or choice kept them from joining the war, they have done nothing to forfeit them. The conqueror cannot take them merely because he subdued someone who forcibly attempted his destruction. He may perhaps claim some goods to repair damage suffered in the war and in defending his rights; we shall shortly examine how far this reaches into the conquered person's possessions. Thus someone who by conquest has acquired a right over another person, allowing him to destroy that person if he pleases, does not by that very conquest acquire a right over the estate to take possession of it and enjoy its benefits. The aggressor's brutal force authorizes his opponent to take his life and destroy him as a harmful creature. Only damage actually sustained gives title to another's goods. I may kill a thief who attacks me on the highway, yet may not do what seems less: take his money and release him. That would make me a robber. His force and resulting state of war forfeited his life but gave me no title to his goods. Conquest therefore extends only to the lives of war's participants, and to their estates only as reparation for damage and war expenses, always reserving the rights of an innocent wife and children.

However fully and completely justice may favour the conqueror, he cannot seize more than the defeated person could forfeit. That person's life lies at the victor's mercy, and his service and goods may be appropriated as reparation. But the victor cannot take his wife and children's goods. They too held rights in the goods he enjoyed and shares in his estate. Suppose, for example, that in the state of nature—and all commonwealths remain in that condition towards one another—I injure someone and refuse compensation. War follows, and my forcible defence of unjust gains makes me the aggressor. I am defeated. My forfeited life is indeed at the victor's mercy, but my wife and children's lives are not. They neither made nor assisted the war. Their lives were not mine to forfeit. My wife had a share in my estate, which I likewise could not forfeit. My children, through their birth, had a right to maintenance from my labour or wealth. The conqueror therefore claims reparation for losses, while the children claim their father's estate for subsistence. As for the wife's share, whether labour or agreement established her title, her husband plainly could not forfeit what belonged to her. What should happen? Nature's fundamental law requires everyone's preservation as far as possible. If the estate cannot satisfy both the conqueror's losses and the children's maintenance, someone who has enough and to spare must surrender part of his full compensation to the more urgent and preferable claim of those who would otherwise perish.

Suppose nevertheless that the conqueror must be repaid every farthing of the war's costs and damage, and that the defeated person's children, deprived of their father's goods, are left to starve. Even then, paying the conqueror's claim would scarcely give him title to any conquered country. The damage caused by war can hardly amount to the value of any substantial tract of land in any region of the world where all the land is already possessed and no part remains unused and available for occupation. I cannot have taken away the conqueror's land, since I have been defeated. Scarcely any other damage could equal the value of my land, assuming equal cultivation and an area approaching that of his territory I overran. Usually the worst destruction amounts to one or two years' produce, seldom four or five. Money and similar stolen treasures are not nature's goods: their value is fanciful and imaginary, not assigned by nature. By her standard they are worth no more than the Americans' wampompeke to a European prince, or European silver money would formerly have been to an American. Five years' produce cannot equal perpetual ownership of land where everything is occupied and nothing remains unused for the dispossessed to take. Once money's imaginary value is removed, this is readily admitted: the disproportion exceeds that between five and five hundred. At the same time, half a year's produce is worth more than an inheritance where more land exists than inhabitants occupy and use, leaving everyone free to take unused land. There, however, conquerors seldom trouble to acquire defeated people's land. No injuries suffered from one another by people in the state of nature—as princes and governments are towards each other—can therefore authorize a conqueror to dispossess the defeated people's descendants. He cannot expel them from an inheritance belonging to them and their descendants through all generations. The conqueror will readily think himself master, and the conquered are in no position to dispute their rights. But if that is all, his title is merely the stronger person's force over the weaker. By that reasoning, whoever is strongest rightfully owns whatever he chooses to seize.

Even in a just war, then, conquest gives no right of dominion over those who fought alongside the conqueror, over inhabitants who did not oppose him, or even over his opponents' descendants. None of these people owes him any subjection as a result of that conquest. If their former government has dissolved, they are free to establish another for themselves.

A conqueror commonly uses his superior force, sword at their breasts, to compel acceptance of his terms and whatever government he chooses to provide. But our question concerns his right to do so. If the answer is that they consent to submit, this admits that their consent is necessary to give him a title to rule. We need then ask only whether promises extorted by unauthorized force count as consent and how far they bind. I say they do not bind at all. Whatever another obtains from me forcibly remains mine by right, and he must immediately restore it. Someone forcibly taking my horse must return it, and I retain the right to recover it. By the same reasoning, someone who forces a promise from me must return it—that is, release me from the obligation—or I may reclaim it myself by choosing whether to perform it. The law of nature binds me only through the rules it prescribes; it cannot bind me through their violation, as happens when something is forcibly extorted. Saying I personally gave the promise changes nothing. My reaching into my pocket and handing over my purse to a thief holding a pistol to my breast neither excuses his force nor transfers my right.

It follows that a conqueror's government does not bind people upon whom it is forcibly imposed if he had no right to wage war against them, or if, despite a rightful war, they took no part against him.

But suppose all the men of that community, as members of the same body politic, are regarded as participants in the unjust war in which they were defeated. Their lives therefore lie at the conqueror's mercy.

I say this does not concern their underage children. A father has no power over his child's life or liberty, so none of his actions can forfeit either. Whatever happened to the fathers, their children are free. The conqueror's absolute power extends only to the actual people he defeated and dies with them. Even if he governs them as slaves under absolute, arbitrary power, he possesses no equivalent dominion over their children. Only the children's own consent can give him power over them, whatever he may force them to say or do. While force rather than choice compels submission, he has no lawful authority.

Every human being comes into the world possessing two distinct rights. First, personal freedom: nobody else has power over his person, whose free disposal belongs to himself. Second, priority over outsiders in inheriting his father's goods together with his brothers.

By the first of these rights, a person is naturally free from subjection to any government, even though the place where he was born lies within that government's jurisdiction. But if he rejects his birth country's lawful government, he must also surrender rights its laws gave him and possessions inherited there from ancestors, provided that government was established by their consent.

Under the second right, inhabitants who descend from the conquered and derive their title to estates from them retain the right to their ancestors' possessions. This remains true even if they do not freely consent to the government whose harsh conditions were forcibly imposed upon the country's owners against their free wishes. The original conqueror never acquired title to the land. Consequently, those descended from people forced under that government's yoke, and anyone claiming through them, always retain a right to shake it off. They may free themselves from the usurpation or tyranny brought upon them by the sword, until their rulers establish a form of government to which they consent willingly and by their own choice. Who doubts that the Grecian Christians, descendants of that country's ancient possessors, may justly throw off the Turkish yoke under which they have so long groaned whenever opportunity permits? No government can have a right to obedience from people who have never freely consented to it. They cannot be assumed to consent until they either enjoy full liberty to choose government and governors, or at least have standing laws freely approved by themselves or their representatives. They must also be allowed their rightful property: they must own what they possess so securely that nobody can take any part without their own consent. Without this, people under any government are not in the condition of free people, but are outright slaves held by the force of war.

Grant, however, what is plainly false: that a conqueror in a just war gains rights over estates as well as power over the conquered persons. No continuing absolute governmental power follows. Their descendants are all free people. If he grants them estates and possessions so they will inhabit his country, which would otherwise be worthless, whatever he grants becomes their property to the extent of the grant. Property's very nature is that it cannot be taken away without its owner's consent.

Their persons are free by an original right belonging to them by nature, and their property, large or small, belongs at their own disposal, not his; otherwise it is not property. Suppose a conqueror grants one man a thousand acres for himself and his heirs forever, and leases another a thousand acres for life at 50_l_. or 500_l_. a year. Does not the first own his thousand acres forever and the second enjoy his for life while paying the rent? Does not the life tenant own everything his labour and industry produce above that rent, even if the surplus is twice its amount? Can anyone say the king or conqueror may afterwards use his conquering power to take some or all of the first man's heirs' land, or the second man's land during his lifetime while rent is paid? May he take either man's goods or money earned from that land whenever he wishes? If so, every free and voluntary agreement becomes void. Sufficient power alone would dissolve any agreement at any time, and powerful people's grants and promises would be mere mockery and deceit. What could be more ridiculous than saying: I give this to you and yours forever, through the surest and most solemn transfer imaginable, yet retain the right to take it back tomorrow if I please?

I shall not now debate whether princes are exempt from their country's laws. I am certain, however, that they remain subject to God's and nature's laws. No person or power can free them from that eternal law's obligations. Promises bind so strongly that even omnipotence can be bound by them. Grants, promises, and oaths are bonds holding the Almighty, whatever flatterers tell worldly princes. Those princes together, even joined by all their people, are compared with the great God only a drop in a bucket or dust on a balance—insignificant, nothing!

The position concerning conquest is briefly this. A conqueror with a just cause has despotical rights over those who actually assisted and joined the war against him. He may recover his losses and costs from their labour and estates, provided he does not injure anyone else's rights. He has no power over inhabitants who did not consent to the war, over captives' children, or over either group's possessions. Conquest therefore gives neither him nor his descendants lawful dominion over them. If he attacks their property, he becomes an aggressor and enters a state of war against them. Neither he nor his successors have any better claim to rule than Hingar or Hubba, the Danes, had in England, or Spartacus would have had if he conquered Italy. Their yoke may be thrown off as soon as God gives the subjected people courage and opportunity. Thus, whatever title the Assyrian kings had acquired over Judah by the sword, God helped Hezekiah cast off that conquering empire's dominion. “And the lord was with Hezekiah, and he prospered; wherefore he went forth, and he rebelled against the king of Assyria, and served him not,” 2 Kings xviii. 7. Plainly, shaking off power established by force rather than right, though called rebellion, is no offence before God. He permits and supports it, even if promises and agreements obtained through force have intervened. Anyone reading Ahaz's and Hezekiah's history carefully will find it very probable that the Assyrians conquered and deposed Ahaz, made Hezekiah king during his father's lifetime, and received Hezekiah's agreed homage and tribute throughout that time.

chapters.title: Chapter 17 — Of Usurpation
paragraphs: If conquest can be called foreign usurpation, usurpation is a kind of domestic conquest, with this difference: a usurper can never be in the right. For there is no usurpation except where one person takes possession of something to which another person has the rightful claim. In itself, it changes only the people governing, not government's forms or rules. If a usurper extends his power beyond what rightfully belonged to the commonwealth's lawful princes or governors, he adds tyranny to usurpation.

In every lawful government, designating the people who will rule is as natural and necessary as determining the form of government itself, and its original establishment comes from the people. Having no governmental form is much the same anarchy as agreeing on monarchy without providing a way to designate the person who will hold power as monarch. Every commonwealth therefore accompanies its established form with rules for appointing those who share public authority and settled procedures for transferring that right to them. For, again, having no form of government is much the same anarchy as agreeing on monarchy without any means of identifying or appointing the person who will possess power and be monarch. Anyone who obtains any share of power through methods other than those prescribed by community law has no right to obedience, even if the commonwealth's form remains intact. He is not the person the laws appointed and consequently not the person the people consented to. Neither such a usurper nor anyone claiming through him can acquire title until the people are both free to consent and have actually consented to recognize and confirm the power he had previously usurped.

chapters.title: Chapter 18 — Of Tyranny
paragraphs: Usurpation exercises power to which someone else has a right; tyranny exercises power beyond right, to which nobody can be entitled. It means using the power in one's hands for his own separate, private advantage rather than for the good of those governed. A governor, whatever his title, then makes his own will the rule instead of law. His commands and actions aim not to preserve his people's property but to satisfy his ambition, revenge, greed, or some other unruly passion.

If anyone doubts the truth or reason of this because it comes from an obscure subject, I hope a king's authority will persuade him to accept it. King James the first told parliament in his speech of 1603:

“In making good laws and constitutions, I shall always prefer the welfare of the public and the entire commonwealth to any private purpose of my own. I always regard the commonwealth's wealth and welfare as my greatest benefit and worldly happiness. This is a point on which a lawful king differs directly from a tyrant. I acknowledge that the special and greatest difference between a rightful king and a usurping tyrant is this: the proud, ambitious tyrant thinks his kingdom and people exist only to satisfy his desires and unreasonable appetites. The righteous, just king, by contrast, recognizes that he exists to secure his people's wealth and property.” Again, in his speech to parliament in 1609, he said:

“The king binds himself by a double oath to observe his kingdom's fundamental laws: tacitly through being king, and thus obliged to protect both the people and their laws; and expressly through his coronation oath. Every just king in an established kingdom must therefore observe the agreement made with his people through his laws, shaping his government accordingly. It resembles God's agreement with Noah after the flood: ‘Hereafter, seed-time and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night, shall not cease while the earth remaineth.’ A king governing an established kingdom therefore ceases to be a king and degenerates into a tyrant as soon as he stops ruling according to his laws.” A little later he adds:

“Every king who is neither a tyrant nor a perjurer will therefore gladly keep within his laws' limits. Those persuading him otherwise are vipers and pests to both king and commonwealth.” Thus that learned king, who understood the nature of things well, locates the difference between king and tyrant solely here: one makes law the boundary of his power and public good the purpose of government; the other makes everything yield to his own will and appetite.

It is mistaken to think this fault belongs only to monarchies. Other forms of government are just as vulnerable to this fault. Wherever power entrusted to govern the people and preserve their property is diverted to other purposes—to impoverish or harass them, or subject them to its holders' arbitrary and irregular commands—it immediately becomes tyranny. It makes no difference whether one person or many exercise it. Thus we read of thirty tyrants at Athens as well as one at Syracuse, and Rome's intolerable rule by the Decemviri was no better.

Where law ends, tyranny begins, if law is violated to another's harm. Anyone in authority who exceeds his legally granted power and uses the force under his command to impose on a subject what law forbids ceases, in that action, to be a magistrate. Acting without authority, he may be opposed like any other person forcibly invading another's rights. This is acknowledged for subordinate magistrates. Someone authorized to arrest me in the street may be resisted as a thief and robber if he tries to break into my house to execute a writ, even though I know his warrant legally authorizes arresting me outside. I would gladly hear why this should not apply to the highest magistrate as well as the lowest. Is it reasonable to suppose that an eldest brother's possession of most of his father's estate entitle him to take his younger brothers' shares? Does a wealthy man's ownership of an entire country entitle him to seize his poor neighbour's cottage and garden whenever he pleases? Lawful possession of power and riches far beyond most of Adam's descendants is no excuse, much less justification, for plunder and oppression, which is what injuring another without authority amounts to. It greatly aggravates the offence. Exceeding authority is no more rightful in a great officer than a minor one, no more justifiable in a king than a constable. It is worse in the king because he has received greater trust, already possesses far more than his brothers, and supposedly understands right and wrong better through the advantages of education, office, and counsellors.

May a prince's commands therefore be opposed? May anyone resist whenever he feels aggrieved and merely imagines he has been treated unjustly? Surely this would unsettle and overthrow every political society, replacing government and order with nothing but anarchy and confusion.

My answer is that force may oppose only unjust and unlawful force. Anyone resisting in any other case brings just condemnation upon himself from both God and humanity. The danger and confusion so often predicted therefore do not follow, for these reasons:

First, in some countries the law makes the prince's person sacred. Whatever he orders or does, his person remains beyond challenge or violence, immune from force and judicial censure or condemnation. Yet the unlawful acts of inferior officers or others acting on his commission may be opposed. The exception is if he actually enters a state of war with his people, dissolving government and leaving them the defence belonging to everyone in the state of nature. Who can predict the outcome then? A neighbouring kingdom has shown the world a strange example. In every other case, the sanctity of his person protects him from these difficulties and, while government continues, from all violence and harm. No constitution could be wiser. The harm that he can inflict through his own personal actions is unlikely to occur very often, or to reach very far among the people. His individual strength cannot overthrow the laws or oppress the people as a body, even if weakness and ill nature make him want to. Particular injuries that may occasionally occur when a headstrong prince takes the throne are amply compensated by public peace and governmental security, with the chief magistrate's person placed beyond danger. The whole body is safer when a few individuals occasionally risk suffering than when the republic's head is readily endangered on slight occasions.

Second, this privilege belongs only to the king's person. It does not prevent questioning, opposing, or resisting those using unjust force, even if they claim a royal commission that the law does not authorize. Consider someone holding the king's writ to arrest a man—a full commission from the king. He still cannot break into that man's house or execute the command on certain days or in certain places, even if the commission states no exceptions. Those restrictions and limits come from the law itself, and a royal commission does not excuse violating them. The king receives his authority only through law. He cannot empower anyone to act against it or justify such action through a commission. A magistrate's command where he lacks authority is as void and meaningless as a private person's. The difference is that a magistrate possesses some authority within defined limits and purposes, while the private person possesses none. Authority, not the commission, confers the right to act; there can be no authority against law. Despite such resistance, both the king's person and his authority remain secure. Neither governor nor government is endangered.

Third, even where the chief magistrate's person is not sacred, allowing resistance to unlawful exercises of his power does not endanger him or embroil government on every slight occasion. If an injured person can obtain relief and compensation through legal appeal, there is no justification for force. Force is permitted only where appeal to law is blocked. Only force that removes that remedy counts as hostile; only it places its user in a state of war and makes resistance lawful. A man holding a sword demands my purse on the highway, although I may have fewer than twelve pence. I may lawfully kill him. To another man I entrust 100 pounds merely while I dismount. Once I have mounted my horse again, I ask him to return the money to me, but he refuses and draws his sword to defend possession if I try to recover it. This man harms me a hundred or perhaps a thousand times more than the first intended, although I killed the first before he actually harmed me. Yet I could lawfully kill the first and cannot lawfully even injure the second. The reason is clear. The first used force threatening my life, leaving no time to appeal to law for protection. After death, appeal would be too late: law cannot restore life to my corpse. To prevent that irreparable loss, the law of nature gave me a right to destroy someone who entered a state of war with me and threatened my destruction. In the second case, my life is not endangered. I may appeal to law and recover my 100 pounds that way.

Fourth, suppose the magistrate uses the power he has acquired to uphold his unlawful actions and uses that same power to obstruct the remedy that the law entitles the injured people to receive. Even against such obvious tyranny, the right of resistance will not suddenly disturb government on slight occasions. If only particular individuals are affected, they may indeed defend themselves and forcibly recover what unlawful force has taken. Yet possessing that right does not readily persuade them to enter a contest in which they are certain to perish. One or a few oppressed people can no more disturb government when the people generally feel unconcerned than a raving madman or headstrong malcontent can overthrow a well-established state. The people are equally unlikely to follow either.

But suppose unlawful acts reach the majority, or harm and oppression fall on only a few in circumstances whose precedents and consequences threaten everyone. If people sincerely believe their laws, and with them their estates, liberties, and lives—and perhaps religion too—are endangered, I cannot say how anyone will prevent resistance to unlawful force. I admit that this difficulty accompanies every form of government whatsoever, once its rulers have brought matters to the point where the people generally suspect their intentions. It is the most dangerous position rulers can create for themselves. They deserve less pity because avoiding it is so easy. A governor sincerely concerned for his people's welfare and the preservation of both them and their laws cannot fail to make them see and feel it, any more than a loving family father can prevent his children from recognizing his love and care.

But suppose everyone sees professions of one kind and actions of another: devices to evade law, and the trust of prerogative—discretionary power in certain matters left with the prince to benefit the people, not harm them—used against its intended purpose. Suppose people find ministers and subordinate magistrates selected for those purposes, then favoured or dismissed according to whether they promote or oppose them. Suppose they see repeated experiments in arbitrary power, and the religion most likely to introduce it secretly favoured while publicly condemned. Its agents receive all possible support, and when support is impossible, continued approval and increased favour. If a long series of actions reveals counsels consistently tending that way, how can anyone avoid becoming convinced of where affairs are going, or considering how to save himself? He can no more avoid that conclusion than a passenger can avoid believing his captain is taking everyone aboard to Algiers when the ship constantly follows that course. Contrary winds, leaks, and shortages of men and provisions may repeatedly force a temporary change of direction, but the captain steadily returns to the same course as soon as wind, weather, and circumstances permit.

chapters.title: Chapter 19 — Of the Dissolution of Government
paragraphs: Anyone who wants to discuss the dissolution of government clearly must first distinguish it from the dissolution of society. What creates a community and brings people out of the unorganized state of nature into one political society is each person's agreement with the others to join together and act as one body, forming a distinct commonwealth. The usual, and almost the only, way this union dissolves is through invasion and conquest by a foreign force. In that situation, the people cannot maintain themselves as one complete, independent body. The union that consisted in their being such a body must therefore end. Each person returns to his previous condition, free to look after himself and secure his safety as he thinks best in some other society. Once society dissolves, its government certainly cannot survive. Thus conquerors' swords often tear governments up by the roots and cut societies to pieces, separating the conquered or scattered multitude from the protection of, and dependence on, the society that should have preserved them from violence. The world knows this way of dissolving governments only too well, and is only too ready to accept it, for further discussion to be necessary. Nor does it take much argument to prove that government cannot remain after society dissolves. That would be as impossible as a house's structure surviving when a whirlwind has scattered its materials, or an earthquake has thrown them into a confused heap.
Besides being overthrown from outside, governments can also dissolve from within.

First, this happens when the legislature is changed. Civil society is a condition of peace among its members. The state of war is excluded by the arbitration they have provided through their legislature to settle any disputes arising among them. The legislature thus unites the members of a commonwealth into one coherent, living body. It is the soul that gives the commonwealth its form, life, and unity. From it the different members gain their mutual influence, sympathy, and connection. When the legislature breaks up or dissolves, dissolution and death follow. For society's essence and union consist in having one will; once established by the majority, the legislature declares and, as it were, holds that will. Establishing the legislature is society's first and fundamental act. It provides for their continuing union under the direction of persons, and the binding force of laws made by persons, whom the people's consent and appointment authorize for that purpose. Without this, no individual or group among them has authority to make laws binding on the rest. If people whom the community has not appointed undertake to make laws, they legislate without authority, and the people are consequently not bound to obey. The people are thereby released from subjection and may establish whatever new legislature they think best. They are entirely free to resist those who use force to impose anything on them without authority. Everyone is free to follow his own will when those entrusted by society to declare the public will are excluded and others, without such authority or delegation, usurp their place.

This usually happens through people in the commonwealth abusing the power they possess. We cannot properly understand it, or know whom to hold responsible, without knowing the form of government involved. Let us therefore suppose that legislative authority requires the agreement of three distinct participants.
(1). One hereditary individual, holding the permanent, supreme executive power, together with authority to summon and dissolve the other two within specified periods of time.
(2). An assembly consisting of hereditary nobles.
(3). An assembly of representatives whom the people elect for a limited term, pro tempore. Given this form of government, it is clear:
