First, when this individual, or prince, substitutes his arbitrary will for the laws—the will of society as declared by its legislature—he changes the legislature. For the effective legislature is the body whose rules and laws are enforced and obedience to which is demanded. If different laws are established, and different rules claimed and enforced, from those enacted by the legislature society established, the legislature has plainly been changed. Whoever introduces new laws without the authority conferred by society's fundamental arrangements, or overturns the old laws, repudiates and overthrows the power that made them. He thereby sets up a new legislature.

Second, the legislature is changed when the prince prevents it from assembling at the proper time or from acting freely to achieve the purposes for which it was established. A legislature does not consist merely in a certain number of people, or even in their meeting together. They must also have freedom to debate and time to complete measures for society's good. When these conditions are removed or altered so that society is deprived of the proper exercise of their power, the legislature is truly changed. Governments are constituted by the use and exercise of the powers their offices were intended to carry, not merely by names. Anyone who removes the legislature's freedom, or prevents it from acting at the appropriate times, effectively removes the legislature itself and brings government to an end.

Third, the legislature is also changed when the prince's arbitrary power changes the electors or the methods of election without the people's consent and against their common interest. If the electors are not those society authorized, or if they choose in a manner different from the one society prescribed, those elected are not the legislature appointed by the people.

Fourth, handing the people over to a foreign power, whether done by the prince or the legislature, certainly changes the legislature and therefore dissolves government. The purpose for which people originally entered into society was to remain one complete, free, independent community governed by its own laws. That purpose is defeated whenever they are placed under another power's control.

It is clear why, under a constitution of this kind, responsibility for dissolving government in these cases falls on the prince. He commands the state's armed force, treasury, and offices. He often persuades himself, or lets others flatter him into believing, that as supreme magistrate he cannot be restrained. He alone can therefore advance far towards these changes under the appearance of lawful authority. He also has the means to intimidate or suppress opponents as factional troublemakers, rebels, and enemies of government. No other part of the legislature, or of the people, can by itself attempt to change the legislature without open, visible rebellion that is readily noticed. When such rebellion succeeds, its effects differ little from foreign conquest. Besides, in this form of government the prince can dissolve the other parts of the legislature, reducing their members to private individuals. They can therefore never change the legislature by law against him or without his agreement: his consent is necessary to give their decisions legal force. Nevertheless, if the other parts of the legislature contribute in any way to an attack on government—either by promoting such designs or by failing to oppose them as far as they can—they are guilty too. They share in what is certainly the greatest crime people can commit against one another.

Sec. 219. There is another way for a government of this kind to dissolve: the holder of supreme executive power neglects and abandons his responsibility until the existing laws can no longer be enforced. This plainly reduces everything to anarchy and effectively dissolves government. Laws are not made for their own sake. Their enforcement binds society together, keeping each part of the political body in its proper place and performing its proper function. When enforcement entirely stops, government visibly stops too, and the people become a confused multitude without order or connection. When justice is no longer administered to secure people's rights, and no power remains within the community to direct its force or provide for public necessities, there is certainly no government left. Laws that cannot be enforced are equivalent to no laws at all. A government without laws is, I suppose, a political mystery beyond human understanding and incompatible with human society.

In these and similar cases, once government dissolves, the people are free to provide for themselves by establishing a new legislature. They may change its members, its form, or both, as they judge best for their safety and welfare. Society can never lose, through another's fault, its natural and original right to preserve itself. That preservation requires an established legislature and fair, impartial enforcement of its laws. Yet the human condition is not so miserable that people cannot use this remedy until it is too late to seek any remedy at all. Telling people they may establish a new legislature after oppression, deception, or surrender to a foreign power has destroyed their old one merely tells them to expect relief when the evil is already beyond cure. In effect, it tells them first to become slaves and then to look after their liberty; once their chains are fastened, it tells them they may act as free people. If that is all it means, it offers mockery rather than relief. People can never be secure against tyranny if they have no means of escape until they are completely subject to it. They therefore have a right not only to escape tyranny but also to prevent it.
Second, therefore, there is another way governments dissolve: either the legislature or the prince acts against the trust placed in them.

First, the legislature violates its trust when it attempts to invade the subjects' property and make itself, or some part of the community, master of the people's lives, liberties, or fortunes, with arbitrary power to dispose of them.

People enter society to preserve their property. They choose and authorize a legislature so that laws and rules will protect the property of every member, limiting the power and restraining the dominion of every part and person within society. We can never suppose that society intends the legislature to have power to destroy what everyone joins society to secure, and for whose protection the people submitted to legislators of their own choosing. Whenever legislators attempt to take away and destroy the people's property, or reduce them to slavery under arbitrary power, they enter a state of war with the people. The people are then released from further obedience and may turn to the common refuge God has provided for everyone against force and violence. Thus, whenever the legislature violates this fundamental rule of society—whether through ambition, fear, folly, or corruption—and attempts to seize for itself, or give anyone else, absolute power over the people's lives, liberties, and estates, its breach of trust forfeits the power the people entrusted to it for entirely different purposes. That power returns to the people. They may reclaim their original liberty and, by establishing whatever new legislature they think appropriate, provide for their own safety and security, the purpose for which they live in society. What I have said about the legislature generally also applies to the supreme executive. He holds a double trust: a share in legislation and supreme responsibility for enforcing the law. He violates both when he tries to make his arbitrary will the law of society. He also violates his trust when he uses society's force, treasury, and offices to corrupt its representatives and win them over to his purposes. The same is true when he openly secures electors' commitments in advance, dictates their choice of candidates whom requests, threats, promises, or other means have brought into his designs, and uses those electors to return people who have already promised how they will vote and what laws they will enact. What does such control of candidates and electors, and such remodelling of elections, do except tear government up by the roots and poison the very source of public security? The people reserved the choice of representatives as a safeguard for their property. Their only purpose could have been to ensure that representatives were always freely chosen and, once chosen, would act and deliberate freely, deciding after examination and mature debate what the commonwealth's needs and the public good required. Those who commit their votes before hearing debate and weighing the arguments on every side cannot do this. Preparing such an assembly, and attempting to install declared supporters of one's own will as the people's true representatives and society's lawmakers, is as complete a breach of trust and as clear a declaration of an intention to overthrow government as could possibly occur. Add rewards and punishments visibly used for this purpose, together with every device of distorted law to remove and destroy those who resist the design and refuse to betray their country's liberties, and there can be no doubt about what is happening. It is easy to determine what power should remain in the hands of those who use it against the trust attached to its original establishment. Anyone must see that a person who has once attempted such a thing can no longer be trusted.

Perhaps someone will object that the people are ignorant and always dissatisfied, and that founding government on their shifting opinions and uncertain moods exposes it to certain ruin. No government, they will say, can last long if the people may establish a new legislature whenever the old one offends them. My answer is: quite the reverse. People are not as easily drawn away from their old forms of government as some suggest. It is difficult even to persuade them to correct acknowledged faults in the arrangement they are used to. Whether defects were present from the beginning or introduced later by time or corruption, changing them is no easy matter, even when everyone sees an opportunity. This slowness and reluctance to abandon old constitutions has, through the many revolutions in this kingdom during this age and earlier ones, kept us with our old legislature of king, lords, and commons, or brought us back to it after an interval of fruitless attempts. Whatever provocations have removed the crown from particular princes' heads, they have never carried the people so far as to place it in another line.
But someone will say that this principle plants the seeds of frequent rebellion. To this I reply:

First, it does so no more than any other principle. When people are made miserable and find themselves exposed to mistreatment by arbitrary power, praise their rulers as sons of Jupiter as loudly as you please. Call them sacred and divine, descended from heaven or authorized by it; represent them as whoever or whatever you choose. The result will be the same. A people widely mistreated in violation of their rights will seize any opportunity to relieve themselves of a burden that weighs heavily on them. They will desire and seek that opportunity, and the changes, weaknesses, and accidents of human affairs seldom take long to provide it. Anyone who has seen no example in his own time must have lived in the world only briefly. Anyone unable to cite examples from every sort of government must have read very little.

Second, such revolutions do not follow every small mistake in managing public affairs. People will endure great errors by their rulers, many bad and troublesome laws, and all the lapses of human weakness without mutiny or complaint. But when a long succession of abuses, evasions, and deceptions all point in the same direction, the people can see the design. They cannot help feeling what they suffer or seeing where they are being led. It is then no surprise if they rouse themselves and try to place government in hands that will secure the purposes for which it was originally established. Without those purposes, ancient names and impressive forms of government are far worse than the state of nature or outright anarchy. The difficulties are just as great and immediate, while the remedy is further away and harder to obtain.

Third, the principle that people may provide anew for their safety through a new legislature, when their legislators violate their trust by invading their property, is the strongest protection against rebellion and the most likely means of preventing it. Rebellion opposes authority, not particular persons, and authority rests solely on the government's constitution and laws. Whoever forcibly breaks those laws and uses force to uphold the violation is truly and properly a rebel. By entering society and civil government, people excluded force and introduced laws to preserve property, peace, and unity among themselves. Those who restore force in opposition to law do rebellare: they bring back the state of war, and are properly called rebels. Those in power are the most likely to do this, given their claim to authority, the temptation presented by the force they command, and the flattery of those around them. The best way to prevent the evil is therefore to show its danger and injustice to those most tempted to commit it.

In both cases already mentioned—changing the legislature or legislators acting against the purpose for which they were established—the offenders are guilty of rebellion. Anyone who forcibly removes a society's established legislature and the laws it has made in fulfilment of its trust removes the arbitration to which everyone consented for peacefully deciding their disputes and excluding the state of war. Those who remove or change the legislature take away this power of final decision, which nobody can possess without the people's appointment and consent. They destroy the authority that the people established, and that nobody else could establish, and introduce a power the people never authorized. They thereby introduce a state of war: force without authority. By removing society's established legislature, whose decisions the people accepted as their own united will, they undo the bond and expose the people once more to the state of war. And if those who forcibly remove the legislature are rebels, the legislators themselves deserve that name no less, as I have shown, when they forcibly attack the people they were appointed to protect and preserve, and attempt to take away their liberties and property. They enter a state of war against those who made them protectors and guardians of their peace. They are therefore properly, and with the greatest aggravation of their offence, rebellantes—rebels.

But perhaps those who say this doctrine lays a foundation for rebellion mean something else. They may say that civil wars or internal disorders could result from telling people they are released from obedience when unlawful attacks are made on their liberties or property, and may resist the unlawful violence of their former magistrates when these invade their property in violation of their trust. The doctrine, they conclude, must be rejected because it destroys the world's peace. On the same grounds, they might as well say honest people must not resist robbers or pirates because resistance could cause disorder or bloodshed. Any harm resulting in such cases should be charged to the person invading his neighbour's rights, not to the person defending his own. If an innocent, honest man must peacefully surrender everything to anyone who violently seizes it, I ask what kind of peace the world will have: one consisting entirely of violence and plunder, maintained solely for robbers' and oppressors' benefit. Who would not call it an admirable peace between the mighty and the weak when a lamb offers its throat without resistance to be torn by an overbearing wolf? Polyphemus's cave supplies a perfect model of this peace and government. Ulysses and his companions had nothing to do but quietly allow themselves to be eaten. No doubt Ulysses, being a prudent man, preached passive obedience and urged peaceful submission, explaining how important peace was to humanity and pointing out the difficulties that might arise if they attempted to resist Polyphemus, who now held power over them.

Government exists for humanity's good. Which is better for humanity: that the people should always lie exposed to the unlimited will of tyranny, or that rulers should sometimes face resistance when they exceed the proper use of power and employ it to destroy their people's property instead of preserving it?

Nor should anyone say this will cause trouble whenever some meddlesome or turbulent person wants to change the government. Such people may indeed stir whenever they please, but only to bring upon themselves the ruin and destruction they deserve. Until the harm becomes widespread, and the rulers' evil designs become visible or their attacks are felt by most people, the people are unlikely to move. They are more inclined to suffer than to obtain justice through resistance. Individual examples of injustice, or the oppression of some unfortunate person here and there, do not move them. But suppose they generally become convinced, on clear evidence, that plans are being pursued against their liberties, and the overall course and direction of events inevitably give them strong suspicions of their rulers' evil intentions. Who is to blame? Who can help it if those who could have avoided suspicion bring it upon themselves? Are the people at fault for having the understanding of rational creatures and judging things as they find and experience them? Does the fault not lie instead with those who create a situation they do not want recognized for what it is? I admit that private individuals' pride, ambition, and restlessness have sometimes caused great disorders in commonwealths, and factions have proved fatal to states and kingdoms. But has the harm more often begun with the people's recklessness and desire to throw off their rulers' lawful authority, or with rulers' arrogance and efforts to acquire and exercise arbitrary power over the people? Did oppression or disobedience first produce the disorder? I leave those questions to impartial history. Of this I am certain: whoever, ruler or subject, forcibly attempts to invade either the prince's or the people's rights, laying the groundwork for overthrowing the constitution and structure of a just government, commits what I consider the greatest crime possible. He must answer for all the bloodshed, plunder, and devastation that breaking governments apart brings upon a country. Whoever does this rightly deserves to be regarded as humanity's common enemy and scourge, and treated accordingly.

Everyone agrees that subjects or foreigners who forcibly attack a people's property may be resisted by force. Yet lately some have denied that magistrates doing the same thing may be resisted. It is as though those enjoying the greatest legal privileges and advantages thereby gained permission to break the very laws that alone placed them above their brothers. Their offence is actually greater: they show ingratitude for the larger share the law gives them and also break the trust their brothers have placed in their hands.

Anyone using force without right—as everyone in society does who uses it without legal authority—enters a state of war with those against whom he uses it. In that state, all previous ties are cancelled and all other rights cease; everyone may defend himself and resist the aggressor. This is so clear that even Barclay, that great champion of kings' power and sacredness, must admit that in some cases the people may lawfully resist their king. He admits it, moreover, in a chapter claiming to show that divine law excludes every kind of rebellion by the people. His own doctrine thus makes clear that, since resistance is sometimes permitted, not every resistance to princes is rebellion. Here are his words. Quod siquis dicat, Ergone populus tyrannicae crudelitati & furori jugulum semper praebebit? Ergone multitude civitates suas fame, ferro, & flamma vastari, seque, conjuges, & liberos fortunae ludibrio & tyranni libidini exponi, inque omnia vitae pericula omnesque miserias & molestias a rege deduci patientur? Num illis quod omni animantium generi est a natura tributum, denegari debet, ut sc. vim vi repellant, seseq; ab injuria, tueantur? Huic breviter responsum sit, Populo universo negari defensionem, quae juris naturalis est, neque ultionem quae praeter naturam est adversus regem concedi debere. Quapropter si rex non in singulares tantum personas aliquot privatum odium exerceat, sed corpus etiam reipublicae, cujus ipse caput est, i.e. totum populum, vel insignem aliquam ejus partem immani & intoleranda saevitia seu tyrannide divexet; populo, quidem hoc casu resistendi ac tuendi se ab injuria potestas competit, sed tuendi se tantum, non enim in principem invadendi: & restituendae injuriae illatae, non recedendi a debita reverentia propter acceptam injuriam. Praesentem denique impetum propulsandi non vim praeteritam ulciscenti jus habet. Horum enim alterum a natura est, ut vitam scilicet corpusque tueamur. Alterum vero contra naturam, ut inferior de superiori supplicium sumat. Quod itaque populus malum, antequam factum sit, impedire potest, ne fiat, id postquam factum est, in regem authorem sceleris vindicare non potest: populus igitur hoc amplius quam privatus quispiam habet: quod huic, vel ipsis adversariis judicibus, excepto Buchanano, nullum nisi in patientia remedium superest. Cum ille si intolerabilis tyrannus est (modicum enim ferre omnino debet) resistere cum reverentia possit, Barclay contra Monarchom. 1. iii. c. 8.
Rendered into English, this reads as follows:

But someone may ask: must the people always expose themselves to tyranny's cruelty and rage? Must they sit still while their cities are plundered and burned to ashes, their wives and children exposed to the tyrant's lust and fury, and themselves and their families brought by their king to ruin and every misery of deprivation and oppression? Must humans alone be denied the common privilege of meeting force with force, which nature so freely grants all other creatures to protect themselves from injury? I answer that self-defence belongs to the law of nature and cannot be denied to the community, even against the king himself. But they must never be allowed to take revenge on him, since that is inconsistent with the same law. If, therefore, the king shows hatred not merely towards certain individuals but towards the commonwealth whose head he is, and cruelly tyrannizes over all or a considerable part of the people with intolerable mistreatment, the people may resist and defend themselves against injury. This qualification must apply: they may defend themselves but must not attack their prince. They may repair the damage suffered, but no provocation permits them to exceed the limits of proper reverence and respect. They may repel the present attack but must not avenge past violence. Defending life and limb is natural; an inferior punishing a superior is contrary to nature. The people may prevent intended harm before it occurs, but once it has occurred they must not avenge it upon the king, even though he committed the wicked act. This distinguishes the people's collective privilege from that of a private individual. Our opponents themselves, except Buchanan, allow individuals no remedy except patience. The people as a body, however, may respectfully resist intolerable tyranny; if it is only moderate, they ought to endure it.
That is how far this great champion of monarchical power permits resistance.
He has, admittedly, attached two limitations to it, both of them useless:
First, he says resistance must be conducted with reverence.

Second, there must be no retribution or punishment, because, he says, an inferior cannot punish a superior. First, it will take some skill to explain how one can resist force without striking back, or strike with reverence. Anyone meeting an assault merely with a shield to receive the blows, or in some still more respectful posture, without a sword in hand to diminish the attacker's confidence and force, will soon reach the end of his resistance. He will find that this defence merely brings worse treatment upon him. This is as ridiculous a method of resisting as Juvenal thought it was of fighting: ubi tu pulsas, ego vapulo tantum—where you do the hitting and I simply take the blows. The contest will inevitably end as he describes it there:

/*[4] -----Libertas pauperis haec est: Pulsatus rogat, et pugnis concisus, adorat, Ut liceat paucis cum dentibus inde reverti. */ This is the poor man's freedom: beaten, he begs; battered by fists, he pleads to be allowed to leave with a few teeth still remaining.

Such imaginary resistance, in which people may not strike back, will always end this way. Anyone allowed to resist must therefore be allowed to strike. Then let our author, or anyone else, accompany a blow to the head or a slash across the face with as much reverence and respect as he pleases. For all I know, anyone able to reconcile blows with reverence may, as a reward for his efforts, wish to receive a polite and respectful beating with a cudgel wherever he can find one.

Second, consider his second claim, that an inferior cannot punish a superior. Generally speaking, this is true while the superior remains superior. But meeting force with force establishes a state of war that puts both parties on equal terms and cancels every previous relationship of reverence, respect, and superiority. The remaining advantage belongs to the person resisting unjust aggression: if he prevails, he has the right to punish the offender both for breaking the peace and for all the evils that followed. Elsewhere Barclay is therefore more consistent with himself and denies that resisting a king is ever lawful. Yet there he specifies two cases in which a king can cease, through his own actions, to be king. These are his words:

Quid ergo, nulline casus incidere possunt quibus populo sese erigere atque in regem impotentius dominantem arma capere & invadere jure suo suaque authoritate liceat? Nulli certe quamdiu rex manet. Semper enim ex divinis id obstat, Regem honorificato; & qui potestati resistit, Dei ordinationi resisit: non alias igitur in eum populo potestas est quam si id committat propter quod ipso jure rex esse desinat. Tunc enim se ipse principatu exuit atque in privatis constituit liber: hoc modo populus & superior efficitur, reverso ad eum sc. jure illo quod ante regem inauguratum in interregno habuit. At sunt paucorum generum commissa ejusmodi quae hunc effectum pariunt. At ego cum plurima animo perlustrem, duo tantum invenio, duos, inquam, casus quibus rex ipso facto ex rege non regem se facit & omni honore & dignitate regali atque in subditos potestate destituit; quorum etiam meminit Winzerus. Horum unus est, Si regnum disperdat, quemadmodum de Nerone fertur, quod is nempe senatum populumque Romanum, atque adeo urbem ipsam ferro flammaque vastare, ac novas sibi sedes quaerere decrevisset. Et de Caligula, quod palam denunciarit se neque civem neque principem senatui amplius fore, inque animo habuerit interempto utriusque ordinis electissimo quoque Alexandriam commigrare, ac ut populum uno ictu interimeret, unam ei cervicem optavit. Talia cum rex aliquis meditator & molitur serio, omnem regnandi curam & animum ilico abjicit, ac proinde imperium in subditos amittit, ut dominus servi pro derelicto habiti dominium. In modern English: What, then: can no situation arise in which the people, by their own right and authority, may help themselves, take up arms, and attack a king who rules over them imperiously? None at all while he remains king. “Honour the king,” and “He who resists the power resists God's ordinance,” are divine declarations that never permit it. The people can therefore acquire power over him only if he does something that makes him cease to be king. He then strips himself of his crown and dignity and returns to the condition of a private individual. The people become free and superior, recovering the power they held during the interregnum before crowning him. Few offences, however, bring matters to this point. After carefully considering the question from every side, I can find only two. There are, I say, two cases in which a king, ipso facto—by the act itself—ceases to be king and loses all royal power and authority over his people. Winzerus also identifies them. The first is when he attempts to overthrow government: when he plans and intends to ruin the kingdom and commonwealth. Thus Nero is recorded as having resolved to destroy Rome's senate and people, devastate the city with fire and sword, and then move elsewhere. Caligula openly declared that he would no longer be head of the people or senate. He planned to kill the most worthy men of both ranks and then withdraw to Alexandria, and wished the people had only one neck so that he could kill them all with one blow. A king who entertains and seriously pursues such designs immediately abandons all care and concern for the commonwealth. Consequently, he forfeits his power to govern his subjects, just as a master loses dominion over slaves he has abandoned.

Alter casus est, Si rex in alicujus clientelam se contulit, ac regnum quod liberum a majoribus & populo traditum accepit, alienae ditioni mancipavit. Nam tunc quamvis forte non ea mente id agit populo plane ut incommodet: tamen quia quod praecipuum est regiae dignitatis amifit, ut summus scilicet in regno secundum Deum sit, & solo Deo inferior, atque populum etiam totum ignorantem vel invitum, cujus libertatem sartam & tectam conservare debuit, in alterius gentis ditionem & potestatem dedidit; hac velut quadam regni ab alienatione effecit, ut nec quod ipse in regno imperium habuit retineat, nec in eum cui collatum voluit, juris quicquam transferat; atque ita eo facto liberum jam & suae potestatis populum relinquit, cujus rei exemplum unum annales Scotici suppeditant. Barclay contra Monarchom. 1. iii. c. 16. In modern English: The other case occurs when a king makes himself dependent on another ruler and places under another's dominion the kingdom his ancestors left him and the people entrusted freely to his hands. Perhaps he does not intend to harm the people. Nevertheless, he has lost the chief element of royal dignity: being supreme in his kingdom, next to and immediately beneath God. He has also betrayed or forced his people, whose liberty he should have carefully preserved, into a foreign nation's power and dominion. By this effective transfer of his kingdom, he loses the power he previously possessed without transferring even the smallest right to those on whom he intended to bestow it. His act therefore frees the people and leaves them to govern themselves. One example appears in the Scotch Annals.

In these cases Barclay, the great champion of absolute monarchy, must admit that a king may be resisted and ceases to be king. Without multiplying examples, the principle is this: wherever he lacks authority, he is no king and may be resisted. Wherever authority ends, his kingship ends too, and he becomes like other people who possess no authority. Barclay's two examples differ little from those I have already described as destroying governments. But he omits the principle underlying his own doctrine: breach of trust, through failure to preserve the agreed form of government and failure to pursue government's purpose, which is the public good and the preservation of property. Once a king has dethroned himself and entered a state of war with his people, what prevents them from proceeding against this former king as against anyone else who has entered a state of war with them? Barclay and those who share his opinion would do well to tell us. I also ask readers to notice Barclay's statement that the people may prevent intended harm before it occurs. He thereby permits resistance while tyranny is still only planned. When a king entertains and seriously pursues such designs, Barclay says, he immediately abandons all care and concern for the commonwealth. According to him, then, neglect of the public good counts as evidence of such a design, or at least as sufficient grounds for resistance. He gives the reason in these words: because he betrayed or forced his people, whose liberty he should have carefully preserved. His addition, “into a foreign nation's power and dominion,” changes nothing. The fault and forfeiture lie in the loss of the liberty he ought to preserve, not in the identity of those to whose dominion the people are subjected. Their rights are equally invaded and their liberty equally lost whether their own nation or a foreign nation enslaves them. That is the injury, and against that alone they possess the right of defence. Examples in every country show that the offence comes from changing the government, not from changing the nationality of the people who govern. Bilson, a bishop of our church and a strong defender of princes' power and prerogative, acknowledges, if I remember correctly, in his treatise on Christian subjection that princes may forfeit their power and their claim to their subjects' obedience. If authorities were needed where reason speaks so clearly, I could direct the reader to Bracton, Fortescue, the author of the Mirrour, and others who cannot be suspected of ignorance of our government or hostility towards it. But I thought Hooker alone might satisfy those who rely on him for their ecclesiastical polity yet, by a strange turn of fate, deny the principles on which he builds it. They had better consider whether cleverer operators are using them as tools to pull down their own structure. Of this I am sure: their civil doctrine is so novel, dangerous, and destructive to rulers and people alike that earlier ages could never tolerate its introduction. We may therefore hope that future ages, freed from the impositions of these Egyptian under-taskmasters, will despise the memory of such servile flatterers. While it seemed to serve their interests, they reduced all government to absolute tyranny and declared everyone born to the slavery for which their own base souls fitted them.

Here the familiar question will probably arise: who is to judge whether the prince or legislature has violated its trust? Perhaps disaffected and factional people will spread that accusation when the prince is merely exercising his proper prerogative. I reply: the people will judge. Who can judge whether a trustee or deputy acts properly and fulfils his trust except the person appointing him? Having appointed him, that person must retain the power to dismiss him when he betrays the trust. If this is reasonable in private individuals' particular affairs, why should it be different in the most important case of all, affecting the welfare of millions? Here the harm, unless prevented, is greater, and obtaining redress is especially difficult, costly, and dangerous.

Furthermore, the question “Who will judge?” cannot mean there is no judge at all. Where no earthly court can decide disputes between people, God in heaven is the judge. He alone, it is true, judges what is right. Yet here, as in every other case, each person must judge for himself whether someone else has entered a state of war with him, and whether he should appeal to the Supreme Judge, as Jeptha did.

Suppose a dispute arises between a prince and some of the people over a matter of great importance on which the law is silent or uncertain. I think the proper arbitrator is the people as a body. Where the prince holds a trust that exempts him from the law's ordinary rules, some may feel injured and believe he is violating or exceeding that trust. Who is better qualified to judge its intended extent than the people who originally entrusted it to him? But if the prince, or whoever administers government, rejects that means of deciding the question, no appeal remains except to heaven. Force between parties with no recognized superior on earth, or force that prevents appeal to any earthly judge, is properly a state of war. In that condition, appeal lies only to heaven. The injured party must then judge for himself when he considers it appropriate to make that appeal and entrust himself to its outcome.

To conclude: the power each individual gives society on joining it can never return to individuals while that society continues. It always remains in the community, because without it there could be no community or commonwealth, contrary to their original agreement. Similarly, when society places legislative power in an assembly to remain with its members and their successors, giving them directions and authority to appoint those successors, that power cannot return to the people while the government continues. By establishing a legislature empowered to continue forever, they have surrendered their political power to it and cannot reclaim it. But matters differ if they have limited their legislature's duration, making supreme power in a person or assembly temporary, or if those holding authority forfeit it through misconduct. On that forfeiture, or when the appointed term expires, power returns to society. The people may then act as the supreme authority and retain legislative power themselves, establish a new form of government, or keep the old form while placing power in new hands, as they think best.
